name: Principality of Zeta
label: serbian principalities
description: The Principality of Zeta was a late medieval South Slavic state ruled by the Crnojević noble house across modern Montenegro and northern Albania. Emerging from the fragmentation of the Serbian Despotate, the principality fiercely defended its mountain heartlands against expanding Ottoman armies while maintaining complex diplomatic ties with the Republic of Venice. Following prolonged resistance from their fortified seats at Žabljak and Cetinje, the rulers were eventually driven into exile and the territory was absorbed into Ottoman administrative sanjaks. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Žabljak Crnojevića; Common languages: Old Serbian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Crnojević; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Serbian Despotate; Succeeded by: Sanjak of Scutari

name: Kingdom of Naples
description: The Kingdom of Naples constituted a major sovereign realm encompassing the southern mainland of the Italian Peninsula following the division of the earlier Norman-Swabian Sicilian realm. Reconstituted under the Trastámara branch of the Crown of Aragon after the death of Alfonso V, the kingdom flourished as a prominent Renaissance cultural and military centre. Although intermittently contested and occupied during the Italian Wars, Naples preserved its distinct dynastic institutions and legal identity until its formal union into the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in 1816. \n\n Status: Sovereign monarchy; Capital: Naples; Common languages: Italian, Neapolitan and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Renaissance; Preceded by: Crown of Aragon; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Two Sicilies

name: Alcácer Ceguer
label: european enclaves in north africa before 1830
description: Alcácer Ceguer was a fortified Portuguese colonial enclave on the northern coastline of Morocco between Tangier and Ceuta. Captured in 1458 under King Afonso V, the strategic circular citadel served as an Atlantic military garrison designed to secure shipping through the Strait of Gibraltar and counter Muslim maritime power. Facing sustained logistical costs and growing encirclement by inland Moroccan forces, the Portuguese crown permanently evacuated and demolished the outpost in 1551. \n\n Status: Colonial garrison; Administrative seat: Ksar es-Seghir; Common languages: Portuguese and Arabic; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military governorship; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Marinid Sultanate; Succeeded by: Wattasid Sultanate

name: County of Hanau-Lichtenberg
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Hanau-Lichtenberg was an imperial estate of the Holy Roman Empire located primarily in lower Alsace and adjacent Upper Rhenish territories. Established through the inheritance of the barony of Lichtenberg by the counts of Hanau, the territory maintained sovereign immediacy within the Upper Rhenish Circle from administrative centres at Babenhausen and Buchsweiler. The county experienced territorial reorganisation during the French Revolutionary wars before its ultimate mediatisation between France and the Grand Duchy of Baden in 1803. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Buchsweiler; Common languages: German and Alsatian; Religion: Lutheranism and Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal principality; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: County of Hanau; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Baden

name: Republic of Ragusa
label: maritime republics
description: The Republic of Ragusa was an aristocratic maritime city-state centred on the fortified Adriatic port of Dubrovnik in southern Dalmatia. During this era, the merchant republic operated as an autonomous tributary client of the Ottoman Empire, paying an annual tribute to the Sultan while retaining full domestic governance and diplomatic neutrality. Ragusa leveraged this unique protectorate status to build a prosperous commercial fleet linking Mediterranean trade routes with the Balkan interior. \n\n Status: Tributary republic; Capital: Ragusa; Common languages: Venetian, Latin, Italian and Croatian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Aristocratic maritime republic; Ruler title: Rector; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Republic of Ragusa; Succeeded by: Republic of Ragusa

name: Mandara Kingdom
description: The Mandara Kingdom was a sovereign Central African state situated in the rugged Mandara Mountains in what is now northern Cameroon. Established by the Wandala people around their early royal settlements at Doulo and Mora, the realm developed sophisticated ironworking traditions and terraced agricultural practices. The kingdom defended its montane borders against encroaching regional neighbours while participating in trade networks linking the Lake Chad basin with the southern savanna. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Mora; Common languages: Wandala; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Tlika; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Mandara Kingdom

name: Marquisate of Zibello
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Zibello was a miniature imperial fief situated in the lowlands of western Emilia along the banks of the Po River. Ruled by a cadet branch of the noble Pallavicino family following the partition of the lands of Rolando the Magnificent, the tiny principality maintained imperial immediacy amidst neighbouring Milanese and Parmense rivals. Although temporarily usurped by the Rangoni family during the sixteenth century, the marquisate survived until its abolition during the Napoleonic restructuring of northern Italy. \n\n Status: Imperial fief; Capital: Zibello; Common languages: Italian and Emilian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal marquisate; Ruling dynasty: Pallavicino; Historical era: Early modern period; Disestablished: 1803; Succeeded by: French Empire

name: County of Scavolino
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Scavolino was a small sovereign enclave of the Holy Roman Empire located in the historical Montefeltro region of central Italy near Pennabilli. Governed by the Oliva family who were later elevated to imperial princes, the statelet retained imperial immediacy and extensive judicial privileges entirely surrounded by the territories of the Papal States. Following temporary Napoleonic disruptions, the autonomous county was restored briefly before being completely incorporated into the Papal States in 1820. \n\n Status: Imperial county; Capital: Pennabilli; Common languages: Italian and Romagnol; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: Oliva; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Duchy of Holstein
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Holstein was an imperial state situated at the southern base of the Jutland peninsula between the Elbe and Eider rivers. Created when King Christian I of Denmark secured the elevation of Holstein-Rendsburg to an imperial duchy in 1474, the territory remained in personal union with the Danish Crown while maintaining formal membership within the Holy Roman Empire. The duchy endured multiple partitions among cadet lines of the House of Oldenburg before being contested in the nineteenth-century Schleswig-Holstein conflicts. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Kiel; Common languages: German, Low German and Danish; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Oldenburg; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Province of Schleswig-Holstein

name: Prince-Provostry of Ellwangen
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Provostry of Ellwangen was an ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire located in northeastern Swabia. Originally founded as a Benedictine abbey in the eighth century, the institution was transformed into a secular college of Augustinian canons regular headed by a prince-provost with imperial immediacy. The principality exercised territorial sovereignty over surrounding towns and forests within the Swabian Circle until its mediatisation and absorption into the Electorate of Württemberg in 1803. \n\n Status: Ecclesiastical principality; Capital: Ellwangen; Common languages: German and Swabian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective ecclesiastical monarchy; Ruler title: Prince-Provost; Historical era: Early modern period; Disestablished: 1803; Succeeded by: Electorate of Württemberg

name: Colony of Cape Verde
description: The Colony of Cape Verde was an insular Portuguese overseas possession comprising ten volcanic islands situated off the western coast of Africa. First settled in the 1460s at Ribeira Grande, the previously uninhabited archipelago was developed into a crucial maritime hub for transatlantic navigation and the early Atlantic slave trade. Administered by Portuguese governors, the colony built a thriving Luso-African Creole culture and economy focused on provisioning caravels, salt extraction and cash-crop agriculture before its later elevation to an overseas province. \n\n Status: Portuguese overseas colony; Capital: Praia; Common languages: Portuguese and Cape Verdean Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial administration; Historical era: Age of Discovery; Preceded by: Uninhabited archipelago; Succeeded by: Overseas Province of Cape Verde

name: Signoria of Senigallia
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Senigallia was a coastal lordly domain in the Marche region of central Italy centred on the fortified Adriatic port of Senigallia. Governed principally by the Della Rovere dynasty under papal and imperial investitures, the small city-state flourished as a strategic commercial harbour and ducal court. Despite being briefly seized by Cesare Borgia during his Romagna campaigns at the turn of the sixteenth century, the lordship maintained local autonomy until its enduring reincorporation into the Duchy of Urbino. \n\n Status: Signoria; Capital: Senigallia; Common languages: Italian and Romagnol; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Lordship; Ruling dynasty: Della Rovere; Historical era: Italian Renaissance; Succeeded by: Duchy of Urbino

name: County of Scheer
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Scheer was an immediate territory of the Holy Roman Empire located along the upper Danube near Sigmaringen in southern Swabia. Held successively by prominent Swabian noble houses, including the counts of Sonnenberg and later the Truchsess von Waldburg-Trauchburg line, the lordship exercised territorial sovereignty and held voting rights in the Swabian Bench of Counts. The small principality retained its distinct feudal prerogatives through the early modern period until being sold to the House of Thurn und Taxis in 1786. \n\n Status: Imperial county; Capital: Scheer; Common languages: German and Swabian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal county; Historical era: Early modern period; Disestablished: 1786; Succeeded by: Principality of Thurn und Taxis

name: Ekpereijie
description: Ekpereijie was an autonomous Edo-speaking precolonial kingdom situated along the northern fringes of the Niger River basin in southwestern Nigeria. Anchored at the royal seat of Ekperi, the polity maintained an organised system of chieftaincies and council governance that preserved communal independence from surrounding regional powers. The kingdom sustained extensive regional trade in agricultural goods, palm oil and local crafts until the expansion of the Royal Niger Company and the British Southern Nigeria Protectorate during the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Ekperi; Common languages: Edo and Ekperi dialects; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Ogie; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: Oil Rivers Protectorate

name: Principality of Abkhazia
description: The Principality of Abkhazia was an autonomous feudal state along the northeastern Black Sea coast that arose following the collapse of the unified Kingdom of Georgia. Governed by the hereditary princes of the Shervashidze dynasty from capitals at Lykhny and Sukhumi, the realm maintained a resilient maritime and mountain society with strong cultural links across western Georgia and the North Caucasus. During this period, the principality successfully safeguarded its local sovereignty against neighbouring Mingrelian and Imeretian dynasts prior to increasing Ottoman naval incursions. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Sukhumi; Common languages: Abkhaz and Georgian; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruling dynasty: Shervashidze; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Georgia; Succeeded by: Ottoman protectorate

name: Bikaner State
description: Bikaner State was a major Rajput kingdom founded in 1465 by Rao Bika, a prince of the Rathore clan of Marwar who carved out an independent realm in the arid Thar Desert region of Jangladesh. Operating from the fortified stronghold of Bikaner, the dynasty secured independence through military prowess, strategic alliances and astute caravan trade management across northwestern Rajasthan. The kingdom maintained sovereign autonomy throughout the regional shifts of northern India until concluding a subsidiary alliance treaty with the British East India Company in 1818. \n\n Status: Princely kingdom; Capital: Bikaner; Common languages: Rajasthani, Bagri, Marwari and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rathore; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Bikaner State (British protectorate)

name: County of East Frisia
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of East Frisia was an immediate imperial territory of the Holy Roman Empire located in the coastal wetlands of northwestern Germany. Established in 1464 when Emperor Frederick III raised Ulrich I of the Cirksena dynasty to an imperial count, the state united contentious coastal chieftaincies and maintained a complex constitutional balance with the powerful estates and the port of Emden. The counts established their permanent residence at Aurich, governing an independent Calvinist and Lutheran land until its eventual transition into an imperial principality. \n\n Status: Imperial county; Capital: Aurich; Common languages: East Frisian Low Saxon, Frisian, Dutch and German; Religion: Calvinism and Lutheranism; Government: Constitutional feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Cirksena; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Principality of East Frisia

name: Dughlat State
description: The Dughlat State was an autonomous Turco-Mongol realm established in the western Tarim Basin following the successful revolt of Mirza Abu Bakr Dughlat against the Chagatai khans in 1465. Centred on the historic oasis cities of Yarkand, Kashgar and Khotan, the breakaway principality operated independently of Moghulistan, fostering regional trade along Silk Road branches. The state maintained strong fortifications and resisted neighbouring steppe armies until its final overthrow by Sultan Said Khan and the formation of the Yarkent Khanate in 1514. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Yarkand; Common languages: Chagatai Turkic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Dughlat clan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Moghulistan; Succeeded by: Yarkent Khanate

name: Kingdom of Kakheti
description: The Kingdom of Kakheti was an independent Georgian monarchy located in eastern Georgia, formed during the tripartite dissolution of the medieval Kingdom of Georgia in 1466. Ruled by a cadet branch of the royal Bagrationi dynasty from their fortified capital at Gremi, the kingdom fostered vibrant agricultural production, silk manufacturing and orthodox monastic culture along the Alazani valley. Kakheti fiercely defended its sovereignty against steppe nomads and neighbouring Persian empires before uniting with the Kingdom of Kartli in 1762 under King Heraclius II. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Gremi; Common languages: Georgian; Religion: Georgian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bagrationi; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti

name: Mudhol State
description: Mudhol State was an autonomous Maratha principality situated in the Deccan plateau along the Ghataprabha River in present-day northern Karnataka. Governed by the Ghorpade dynasty, a distinguished Maratha warrior lineage claiming descent from the Sisodia Rajputs, the state maintained strategic independence while serving as prominent regional commanders during the conflicts of the Bahmani and Bijapur sultanates. The rulers preserved local political authority and land revenue systems at their capital of Mudhol until entering into a protectorate agreement with the British East India Company in 1818. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Mudhol; Common languages: Marathi and Kannada; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ghorpade; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Mudhol State (British protectorate)

name: Sultanate of Touggourt
description: The Sultanate of Touggourt was an independent desert state established in the northern Sahara across the fertile palm groves of the Oued Righ valley in eastern Algeria. Founded by the Berber dynasty of the Banu Djellab after severing ties with the declining Hafsid Sultanate, the realm prospered by controlling trans-Saharan caravan routes, date harvesting and oasis water networks. The sultanate maintained political sovereignty from its walled citadel at Touggourt until an Ottoman military expedition from Algiers reduced the realm to a tributary status in 1552. \n\n Status: Desert sultanate; Capital: Touggourt; Common languages: Berber and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary sultanate; Ruling dynasty: Banu Djellab; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Regency of Algiers

name: Wattasid Dynasty
description: The Wattasid Dynasty was a Zenata Berber sultanate that established rule over northern Morocco following the violent overthrow of the Marinid Sultanate in Fez during the 1460s. Previously serving as influential royal viziers, the Wattasids assumed full sovereign authority under Sultan Abu Abd Allah al-Sheikh Muhammad, though their power was largely confined to urban centres and the coastal hinterlands. The regime faced continuous naval pressures from Portuguese enclaves and mounting popular opposition from the southern Saadi movement, which eventually eclipsed and disestablished the dynasty in 1554. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Fez; Common languages: Arabic and Berber languages; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Wattasid; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Marinid Sultanate; Succeeded by: Saadi Sultanate

name: State of the Teutonic Order
label: states emerged from the northern crusades
description: The State of the Teutonic Order in this era comprised the reduced monastic territory in eastern Prussia that became a formal fief of the Polish Crown under the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466. With the historic seat at Marienburg ceded to Poland, the Grand Masters relocated their administrative centre to Königsberg, swearing oaths of fealty to the Polish monarch. The crusader theocracy persisted as a dependent military order until Grand Master Albert of Brandenburg converted to Lutheranism and secularised the domain into the hereditary Duchy of Prussia in 1525. \n\n Status: Monastic state and Polish fief; Capital: Königsberg; Common languages: German, Low German and Polish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective theocratic monastic order; Ruler title: Grand Master; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: State of the Teutonic Order; Succeeded by: Duchy of Prussia

name: Great Horde
label: successors of the mongol empire
description: The Great Horde was the direct steppe successor khanate of the Golden Horde, centred along the lower Volga and Don rivers with its capital at Sarai. Under the leadership of Khan Ahmed, the realm claimed supreme imperial authority over the fractured Tatar khanates and attempted to enforce tribute collection across the Russian lands. The horde's geopolitical dominance collapsed following the bloodless confrontation at the Ugra River in 1480, after which sustained campaigns by the allied Crimean Khanate finally destroyed the state in 1502. \n\n Status: Steppe khanate; Capital: Sarai; Common languages: Kipchak Turkic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary khanate; Ruling dynasty: Genghisid; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Golden Horde; Succeeded by: Crimean Khanate

name: Khanate of Astrakhan
description: The Khanate of Astrakhan during this initial phase functioned as an autonomous Tatar realm in the lower Volga delta while remaining nominally subordinate to the Great Horde. Founded in the 1460s by Mahmud bin Küchük, the state controlled crucial riverine trade networks connecting the Caspian Sea with northern Eurasian markets from its fortified capital at Xacitarxan. Although frequently subjected to political interference and military incursions by neighbouring Crimean and Nogai rivals, the khanate consolidated its separate dynastic identity until the final dissolution of the Great Horde. \n\n Status: Nominal possession and khanate; Capital: Astrakhan; Common languages: Kipchak Turkic and Nogai; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary khanate; Ruling dynasty: Toqa-Temürid; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Golden Horde; Succeeded by: Khanate of Astrakhan (independent)

name: Malpur State
description: Malpur State was a small autonomous Rajput principality located within the hilly Mahi Kantha region of present-day northeastern Gujarat. Established in 1466 by Rawal Virsinhji, a descendant of the Rathore dynasty of Idar, the state maintained independence through difficult terrain and defensive alliances with neighbouring Gujarati and Mewari rulers. The principality preserved its local revenue administration and traditional feudal customs against the expanding hegemony of the Gujarat Sultanate and later regional powers until entering diplomatic agreements with the British during the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Malpur; Common languages: Gujarati and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rathore; Ruler title: Rawal; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Malpur State (British protectorate)

name: Grand Duchy of Moscow (Military Occupation)
description: The Grand Duchy of Moscow Military Occupation comprised the territories placed under Muscovite martial administration during grand ducal campaigns against neighbouring Tatar khanates and rival principalities. Directed by the field commanders and governors of Grand Prince Ivan III, these temporary occupation administrations oversaw strategic fortresses, seized logistical corridors and enforced loyalty along volatile borderlands such as the Kazan frontier. Rather than functioning as civilian administrative entities, these zones served as temporary staging bases to project military power before formal annexation or client installations. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile expeditionary headquarters; Common languages: Russian and Church Slavonic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Military occupation administration; Head of state: Grand Prince of Moscow; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Khanate of Kazan; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Moscow

name: Hosokawa Clan
description: The Hosokawa Clan during the Ōnin War functioned as the dominant sovereign faction of the Eastern Army in central Japan under the leadership of deputy shogun Hosokawa Katsumoto. Operating primarily from the imperial capital of Kyoto and surrounding family estates in the Kinai region, the clan commanded a vast coalition of loyal daimyō in a devastating conflict over Ashikaga shogunal succession. The prolonged street warfare and political stalemate shattered the central authority of the Muromachi shogunate, inaugurating the prolonged decentralised warfare of the Sengoku period. \n\n Status: Feudal clan territory; Capital: Kyoto; Common languages: Late Middle Japanese; Religion: Shinto and Zen Buddhism; Government: Military clan lordship; Ruling dynasty: Hosokawa; Historical era: Sengoku period; Preceded by: Ashikaga shogunate; Succeeded by: Sengoku daimyō domains

name: Kazakh Khanate
description: The Kazakh Khanate was a vast nomadic empire established across the Central Asian steppes by Janibek Khan and Kerei Khan following their secession from the Uzbek Khanate in the 1460s. Encompassing pasturelands stretching from the Ural River to the Altai foothills, the confederation consolidated distinct Kazakh tribal groupings under a mobile pastoral economy and Genghisid legal traditions. The khanate flourished as a dominant steppe power from administrative and spiritual centres such as Saraishyq and Turkistan, successfully checking Oirat and Uzbek incursions before later fragmenting into three juz. \n\n Status: Nomadic empire; Capital: Turkistan; Common languages: Kazakh, Kipchak Turkic and Chagatai; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Semi-elective monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Genghisid; Ruler title: Khan; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Kazakh Zhuzes

name: Yamana Sōzen Controlled
description: The Yamana Sōzen Controlled territory represented the sovereign domain and military coalition of the Western Army during the devastating Ōnin War in fifteenth-century Japan. Led by the powerful daimyō Yamana Sōzen from his fortified headquarters at Nishijin in northwestern Kyoto, this alliance contested the authority of the Hosokawa faction and the Ashikaga shogunate. The protracted urban battles reduced much of the capital to ashes and crippled national administration, leaving the Western coalition fragmented following Sōzen's death and accelerating the country's descent into Sengoku fragmentation. \n\n Status: Feudal military faction; Capital: Nishijin; Common languages: Late Middle Japanese; Religion: Shinto and Buddhism; Government: Military clan alliance; Ruling dynasty: Yamana; Historical era: Sengoku period; Preceded by: Ashikaga shogunate; Succeeded by: Sengoku daimyō domains

name: Arghun Dynasty
description: The Arghun Dynasty was a Turco-Mongol ruling house that established an independent principality spanning southern Afghanistan, Baluchistan and Sindh. Originating as Timurid governors in Kandahar under Dhu'l-Nun Beg Arghun, the family migrated southward under relentless pressure from the nascent Uzbeks and Babur's expanding power. Re-establishing their sovereign monarchy at Thatta and Bukkur after toppling the native Samma dynasty in 1520, the Arghun rulers governed lower Indus commerce and agriculture until being supplanted by their Tarkhan kinsmen in the mid-sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign dynasty; Capital: Thatta; Common languages: Persian and Sindhi; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Arghun; Ruler title: Shah; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Samma dynasty; Succeeded by: Tarkhan dynasty

name: Kingdom of Kandy
description: The Kingdom of Kandy was an independent Sinhalese realm established in the central highlands of Sri Lanka by Senasammata Vikramabahu following his rebellion against the coastal Kingdom of Kotte. Protected by dense tropical forests and formidable mountain passes, the kingdom developed into the principal bastion of traditional Sinhalese martial culture and Theravada Buddhism. Kandy successfully repulsed repeated invasion attempts by Portuguese and Dutch colonial forces for centuries, maintaining unbroken native sovereignty until the Kandyan Convention with Great Britain in 1815. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kandy; Common languages: Sinhala and Tamil; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Kandyan period; Preceded by: Kingdom of Kotte; Succeeded by: British Ceylon

name: BaLete
description: The BaLete was a sovereign South African chiefdom of Nguni origin that established an enduring home among the Tswana polities of southeastern Botswana. Governed by their traditional paramount king, or Kgosikgolo, the BaLete preserved their distinct cultural identity, military cohesion and clan institutions despite participating in broad Tswana regional affairs. Centred at Ramotswa along the Notwane River, the kingdom engaged in cattle pastoralism and resilient regional defence until being integrated into the British Bechuanaland Protectorate in 1885. \n\n Status: Sovereign chiefdom; Capital: Ramotswa; Common languages: Setswana and Balete dialects; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Kgosikgolo; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Disestablished: 1885; Succeeded by: Bechuanaland Protectorate

name: BaRôlông
description: The BaRôlông was a major precolonial Batswana chiefdom that exercised sovereign authority across the rolling grassland margins of modern northern South Africa and southern Botswana. Governed from significant settlements including Mafikeng and Khunwana by their hereditary paramount rulers, the state maintained sophisticated cattle pastoralism, ironworking and judicial assemblies known as kgotla. The BaRôlông successfully defended their territorial lands against regional rivals and encroaching Boer commandos until formal incorporation into the British imperial sphere via the Bechuanaland Protectorate in 1885. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Mafikeng; Common languages: Setswana; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Kgosi; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Disestablished: 1885; Succeeded by: Bechuanaland Protectorate

name: Colony of São Tomé and Príncipe
description: The Colony of São Tomé and Príncipe was a Portuguese insular territory established in the Gulf of Guinea off the equatorial coast of Central Africa. Uninhabited prior to the arrival of Portuguese navigators in 1470, the fertile volcanic islands were rapidly colonised and transformed into the world's leading sugar producer powered by enslaved African labour. The colony served as a vital naval victualling station and slave entrepôt for transatlantic commerce before diversifying into cacao and coffee production in later centuries. \n\n Status: Overseas colony; Capital: São Tomé; Common languages: Portuguese and Forro Creole; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Age of Discovery; Preceded by: Uninhabited archipelago; Succeeded by: Democratic Republic of São Tomé and Príncipe

name: Iximché
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Iximché was a fortified pre-Columbian city-kingdom established as the capital of the Kaqchikel Maya in the western highlands of Guatemala. Founded around 1470 on a defensible plateau surrounded by deep ravines following a split from the neighbouring Kʼicheʼ realm, the polity was governed jointly by four noble lords drawn from prominent royal lineages. The city-state flourished as a political, military and ceremonial hub with sophisticated masonry temples and ballcourts until Spanish conquistadors occupied and destroyed the stronghold in 1524. \n\n Status: City-kingdom; Capital: Iximche; Common languages: Kaqchikel Maya; Religion: Maya religion; Government: Aristocratic oligarchy; Ruler title: Ahpozotzil and Ahpoxahil; Historical era: Late Postclassic Mesoamerica; Disestablished: 1524; Succeeded by: Captaincy General of Guatemala

name: Signoria of Forlimpopoli
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Forlimpopoli was a small medieval lordship situated in the historic Romagna region of northern Italy along the Via Emilia between Forlì and Cesena. Governed principally by the Zampeschi family as a petty imperial and papal fief, the town commanded important agricultural lands and toll routes across the surrounding lowlands. The signoria maintained its local judicial independence and fortified ducal residence until the extinction of its ruling lineage in 1579 led to full annexation by the Papal States. \n\n Status: Signoria; Capital: Forlimpopoli; Common languages: Italian and Romagnol; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Lordship; Ruling dynasty: Zampeschi; Historical era: Italian Renaissance; Disestablished: 1579; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Sultanate of Pahang
description: The Sultanate of Pahang was a prominent Malay Muslim realm situated along the eastern coast of the Malay Peninsula centred on the fertile Pahang River basin. Established by Sultan Muhammad Shah, a prince of the Malacca Sultanate, the realm asserted increasing independence and developed into a wealthy maritime trading state noted for its alluvial gold and tin deposits. Operating from the royal seat at Pekan, Pahang defended its regional autonomy against European colonial incursions and neighbouring rivals before entering into a personal union with Johor in the 1620s. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Pekan; Common languages: Classical Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Melaka-Pahang dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Johor Empire

name: Wanmaw State
label: shan states
description: Wanmaw State, historically known also as Man Maw or Bhamo, was an outlying Shan principality located in the upper Irrawaddy basin of modern Kachin State in northern Myanmar. Separated from the southern plateau Shan states, the kingdom controlled vital riverine terminals and overland caravan routes linking the Burmese interior with Yunnanese trade networks in southwestern China. Governed by a hereditary saopha, Wanmaw maintained precarious independence amidst alternating invasions and tributary demands from the Ava Kingdom, the Ming Empire and subsequent Burmese dynasties until its final eighteenth-century subjugation. \n\n Status: Shan principality; Capital: Bhamo; Common languages: Shan, Burmese and Chinese dialects; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Konbaung dynasty

name: Portuguese Gold Coast

description: The County of Barby was an immediate imperial territory of the Holy Roman Empire located at the confluence of the Elbe and Saale rivers in modern Saxony-Anhalt. Ruled by the ancient House of Barby and Mühlingen from their residential castle at Barby, the small county exercised territorial sovereignty, tolls on river shipping and agricultural oversight. The counts embraced the Lutheran Reformation during the sixteenth century and maintained their imperial immediacy until the extinction of the male line in 1659, whereupon the county was absorbed by the Duchy of Saxe-Weissenfels. \n\n Status: Imperial county; Capital: Barby; Common languages: German and Low German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Feudal county; Ruling dynasty: House of Barby; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Early modern period; Disestablished: 1659; Succeeded by: Duchy of Saxe-Weissenfels

name: Musikot
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: Musikot was an autonomous hill kingdom belonging to the Chaubisi Rajya group situated in the rugged middle hills of western Nepal. Governed by a hereditary Hindu dynasty of the Khas nobility from its fortified seat at Musikot, the state oversaw agrarian terracing, cattle husbandry and regional mountain barter trade along the Badighat valley. The kingdom preserved its traditional local governance and defensive forts despite periodic boundary conflicts with surrounding petty realms, maintaining independence until being conquered and incorporated during the Gorkhali territorial expansion in 1787. \n\n Status: Chaubisi kingdom; Capital: Musikot; Common languages: Nepali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sen; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Disestablished: 1787; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal

name: Sublime Ottoman State and Crimean Khanate (Military Occupation)
description: The Sublime Ottoman State and Crimean Khanate Military Occupation comprised the Polish-Lithuanian border territories of Podolia and Red Ruthenia held under joint Ottoman and Tatar martial control during the summer and autumn campaigns of 1498. Launched in retaliation for Polish incursions into Moldavia, combined Ottoman-Tatar expeditionary forces ravaged the Dniester basin, capturing major fortresses and establishing temporary operational garrisons across the Galician frontier. The joint military administration operated as a temporary raiding and security perimeter to secure supply lines and extract tribute before withdrawing southward across the Prut River. \n\n Status: Joint military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile allied field command; Common languages: Ottoman Turkish and Crimean Tatar; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Joint military command; Head of state: Ottoman Sultan and Crimean Khan; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Kingdom of Poland; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Poland

name: Daspalla State
description: Daspalla State was an autonomous Hindu principality set across the forested hills and fertile valleys of the Mahanadi River in modern Nayagarh district of Odisha. Founded in 1498 by Raja Salo Bhanj of the Bhanj royal lineage following a partition of the family domain, the state established its administrative capital at Kunjabangarh. The kingdom defended its rugged mountain boundaries, managed timber and agricultural revenues and fostered traditional Odia culture and Jagannath worship until entering into a tributary protectorate agreement with the British East India Company in 1803. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Daspalla; Common languages: Odia; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bhanj; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Daspalla State (British protectorate)

name: Laccadive Islands
description: The Laccadive Islands during this era functioned as a fortified Portuguese colonial dependency situated in the Arabian Sea off the Malabar Coast of southwestern India. Seized by Portuguese naval expeditions in the late 1490s following Vasco da Gama's arrival in Calicut, the archipelago served as a strategic maritime station for securing the lucrative coir rope production and safeguarding oceanic spice lanes. Portuguese rule was administered through small military garrisons stationed at Kavaratti and Amini until persistent local resistance culminated in the expulsion and massacre of the colonisers in 1545. \n\n Status: Portuguese insular colony; Administrative seat: Kavaratti; Common languages: Portuguese, Malayalam and Jeseri; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Sunni Islam; Government: Colonial military post; Historical era: Age of Discovery; Succeeded by: Arakkal Kingdom

name: Swabian League
description: The Swabian League was a powerful mutual defence and peacekeeping confederation of imperial estates, including free imperial cities, prelates and princes across the historical stem duchy of Swabia. Mobilised in early 1499 during the opening phase of the Swabian War, the league operated without a single civil capital, deploying unified military contingents under imperial commanders to counter Swiss Confederate expansionism along the upper Rhine. Although sustaining heavy casualties in winter skirmishes, the league's collective military organisation formed a cornerstone of imperial security and Habsburg regional policy throughout the late fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Military confederation; Administrative seat: Mobile league council; Common languages: German and Swabian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Federal military alliance; Legislature: League Assembly; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Established: 1488; Disestablished: 1534

name: Swiss Confederacy (Military Occupation)
description: The Swiss Confederacy Military Occupation encompassed the border bailiwicks and contested alpine valleys held under Swiss Confederate martial control during the Swabian War and the initial Italian campaigns of 1499. Stationed across the upper Rhine valley, Sundgau and the southern approaches to the Duchy of Milan, confederate expeditionary forces established fortified garrisons to extract wartime requisitions, secure mountain passes and neutralise Habsburg supply lines. These zones operated under temporary communal military commissaries appointed by the Federal Diet, serving as temporary security regimes until peace treaties or territorial cessions finalised status. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: Mobile confederate military command; Common languages: Alemannic German and Lombard; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Confederate military occupation; Legislature: Tagsatzung; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Preceded by: Holy Roman Empire; Succeeded by: Old Swiss Confederacy

name: Emirate of Pazooka
label: kurdish principalities
description: The Emirate of Pazooka, also known as the Pazuki Principality, was an autonomous Kurdish state established in 1499 across the high plateaus of eastern Anatolia between Eleskirt, Malazgirt and Nakhchivan. Founded by the Pazuki tribal confederation during the collapse of the Aq Qoyunlu, the emirate commanded crucial trade and military routes crossing the Armenian Highlands from its capital at Eleskirt. The emirs navigated complex alliances between the expanding Ottoman and Safavid empires, providing skilled cavalry forces while preserving domestic tribal autonomy until their realm was formally absorbed by the Ottoman Empire in 1587. \n\n Status: Kurdish emirate; Capital: Eleskirt; Common languages: Kurdish, Armenian and Turkish; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruling dynasty: Pazuki; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Aq Qoyunlu; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Keladi Kingdom
description: The Keladi Kingdom, also known as the Nayakas of Keladi or Bednore, was an important post-medieval South Indian realm situated in the lush Malnad region of the Western Ghats in modern Karnataka. Established in 1499 by Chowdappa Nayaka as a loyal feudatory of the Vijayanagara Empire, the dynasty subsequently declared full independence following the empire's collapse in 1565. Governed successively from Keladi, Ikkeri and Bidanur, the Veerashaiva monarchs defended coastal trade, fostered Kannada literature and repulsed Mughal and Portuguese incursions until their annexation by the Kingdom of Mysore in 1763. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ikkeri; Common languages: Kannada; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Nayakas of Keladi; Ruler title: Nayaka and Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Preceded by: Vijayanagara Empire; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Mysore

name: Agona
description: Agona was an autonomous precolonial Akan state situated in the coastal hinterlands of modern southern Ghana along the Ayensu River basin. Anchored at its political centre of Agona Swedru, the kingdom was organised around traditional matrilineal clans and governed by a paramount ruler, the Omanhene, assisted by a council of wing chiefs. The state prospered by controlling trade routes linking the Atlantic coastline with inland forest markets, trading salt, fish and agricultural commodities until being drawn into broader conflicts with the expanding Fante and Akwamu confederacies in the seventeenth century. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Agona Swedru; Common languages: Akan; Religion: Traditional Akan religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Omanhene; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Disestablished: 1621; Succeeded by: Fante Confederacy

name: Akyem Abuakwa
description: Akyem Abuakwa was a major precolonial Akan kingdom situated in the fertile forest hills of the Eastern Region of present-day Ghana. Established by the Ofori Panin royal lineage following migrations from the ancient Adansi heartland, the kingdom was administered from its royal capital at Kyebi under a sacred paramount ruler titled the Okyehene. The realm was famous for its rich alluvial goldfields, oil palm cultivation and formidable military organisation, tenaciously defending its political independence against the Ashanti Empire until concluding a protectorate agreement with the British Gold Coast in the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Traditional kingdom; Capital: Kyebi; Common languages: Akan; Religion: Traditional Akan religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ofori Panin; Ruler title: Okyehene; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Succeeded by: Gold Coast Protectorate

name: Baghat State
description: Baghat State was an autonomous Rajput principality located within the rugged Simla Hills of modern Himachal Pradesh in northern India. Founded in the late fifteenth century by Raja Basant Pal of the Pawar Rajput dynasty from Dharanagri, the state controlled fertile mountain valleys and vital transit routes through the lower Himalayas from historic seats at Jaunaji and Bhoch. The principality preserved its local revenue customs and clan autonomy amidst regional upheavals, resisting neighbouring Gurkha invasions before briefly falling under British doctrine of lapse administration in the mid-nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Solan; Common languages: Pahari and Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Pawar; Ruler title: Rana; Historical era: Early modern period; Succeeded by: Baghat State (British protectorate)

name: Baro-Bhuyan Confederacy
description: The Baro-Bhuyan Confederacy was a formidable alliance of autonomous soldier-landowners, or bhuiyans, established across the riverine delta of eastern Bengal and Assam. Operating from historical river strongholds including Sonargaon, these independent chiefs coalesced during periods of regional fragmentation to defend their estates against encroaching Muslim sultanates, Ahom kings and tribal incursions. The confederation maintained a powerful war-boat flotilla, collected agricultural revenues and upheld local Hindu and Muslim traditions, functioning as a de facto sovereign league until being subdued during the centralisation drives of the Bengal Sultanate and subsequent empires. \n\n Status: Aristocratic confederacy; Capital: Sonargaon; Common languages: Bengali and Assamese; Religion: Hinduism and Islam; Government: Confederate oligarchy; Ruler title: Bhuiyan and Raja; Historical era: Late Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Bengal Sultanate

name: Cainta
label: barangay states
description: Cainta was an autonomous precolonial Tagalog barangay state situated along the banks of the Cainta River near the eastern shores of Laguna de Bay in modern Rizal province, Philippines. Enclosed by extensive bamboo stockades and earthworks known as a moog, the settlement was defended by warrior forces wielding bronze cannons, or lantakas, and sharp blowguns. The polity controlled vital riverine commerce linking inland lake communities with the coastal trade of Manila until Spanish conquistador Juan de Salcedo stormed and destroyed the fortified town in August 1571. \n\n Status: Precolonial barangay state; Capital: Cainta; Common languages: Old Tagalog; Religion: Anitism; Government: Barangay chieftaincy; Ruler title: Datu; Historical era: Precolonial Philippines; Disestablished: 1572; Succeeded by: Captaincy General of the Philippines

name: Confederation of the Seven Kingdoms of Kongo dia Nlaza
description: The Confederation of the Seven Kingdoms of Kongo dia Nlaza was an autonomous union of ancient states situated in west Central Africa along the Kwale and Kwango river valleys. Also recorded in contemporary Portuguese chronicles as the Momboares, the confederation was famous throughout the region for its sophisticated raffia cloth weaving and extensive agricultural trade networks linking the Pool Malebo with Atlantic markets. The realm maintained traditional clan governance and local monarchical institutions until being formally annexed into the eastern province of Mbata under King Álvaro II of the Kingdom of Kongo. \n\n Status: Traditional confederation; Capital: Kongo dia Nlaza; Common languages: Kikongo; Religion: Traditional Central African religion; Government: Traditional confederation; Historical era: Precolonial Africa; Disestablished: 1581; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Kongo

name: Dapitan
label: barangay states
description: Dapitan was a flourishing coastal thalassocracy and barangay settlement situated along the north-western coast of Mindanao. Established by Boholano migrants following the destruction of the Kedatuan of Dapitan on Bohol, the community maintained strategic maritime trade networks across the Sulu Sea and the Visayas. Local governance functioned through autonomous datu leadership until Spanish expeditionary forces incorporated the territory into the Captaincy General of the Philippines during the late sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Autonomous barangay state; Capital: Dapitan; Common languages: Subanon and Visayan; Religion: Indigenous animism; Government: Chieftaincy; Historical era: Precolonial Philippines; Established: c. 1500; Disestablished: 1576; Succeeded by: Spanish East Indies

name: Domba
label: comoros sultanates;polities of the swahili coast
description: Domba was a traditional Swahili sultanate located on the southern slopes of the island of Grande Comore. Governed by hereditary noble lineages known as mfaume, the principality drew economic vitality from Indian Ocean maritime commerce and local volcanic agricultural terraces. It retained fierce local autonomy amidst persistent island factionalism until French colonial authorities federated the Comorian sultanates under a unified protectorate in the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Domba; Common languages: Comorian and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional hereditary monarchy; Historical era: Early modern Africa; Established: c. 1500; Disestablished: 1887; Succeeded by: French Comoros

name: Hamahame
label: comoros sultanates;polities of the swahili coast
description: Hamahame was a prominent coastal sultanate situated in the north-eastern region of Grande Comore. Centred upon the fortified port of Mbeni, the polity engaged in active regional commerce across the Mozambique Channel while balancing alliances against competing realm lords on the island. Its sovereign dynastic authority endured across several centuries of Swahili maritime trading before succumbing to internal political consolidation and subsequent French colonial pacification in 1887. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Mbeni; Common languages: Comorian and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic sultanate; Historical era: Early modern Africa; Established: c. 1500; Disestablished: 1887; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Ngazidja

name: Hambuu
label: comoros sultanates;polities of the swahili coast
description: Hambuu was an influential coastal sultanate established along the south-western littoral of Grande Comore. Operating from its administrative seat at Mitsoudje, the realm commanded fertile volcanic slopes and participated extensively in regional Swahili maritime commerce. Local sultans routinely mobilised aristocratic assemblies to protect territorial autonomy until nineteenth-century dynastic wars culminated in the unificatory reign of Sultan Said Ali and the imposition of a French protectorate. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Mitsoudje; Common languages: Comorian and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Islamic sultanate; Historical era: Early modern Africa; Established: c. 1500; Disestablished: 1887; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Ngazidja

name: Hotu Iti
label: easter island polities
description: Hotu Iti was a major indigenous clan realm that exercised paramount control over the south-eastern portion of Easter Island. Centred historically around the monumental megalithic sanctuary of Ahu Tongariki and the quarry at Rano Raraku, the polity directed extensive stone-carving efforts and ceremonial moai construction. The kingdom contested supreme insular hegemony against the rival western Ko Tuu confederacy until ecological exhaustion and catastrophic inter-tribal warfare disrupted traditional lineage kingship during the eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal kingdom; Administrative seat: Tongariki; Common languages: Rapa Nui; Religion: Polynesian animism; Government: Traditional clan kingship; Historical era: Polynesian Middle Ages; Established: c. 1500; Disestablished: 1771; Historical region: Polynesia

name: Hsipaw State
label: shan states
description: Hsipaw State was a powerful Shan principality centred in the mountainous river valleys of northern Upper Burma. Under the governance of hereditary saophas, the state held command over critical highland overland trade routes connecting the Irrawaddy basin with Yunnan. It frequently asserted military independence against neighbouring Burmese courts until the surging expansionism of King Bayinnaung of the Taungoo Empire brought the principality into tributary vassalage during the late 1550s. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Hsipaw; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: c. 13th century; Disestablished: 1558; Succeeded by: Taungoo Empire

name: Igorot
label: barangay states
description: Igorot was an autonomous confederation of highland tribal communities spanning the rugged Cordillera Central of northern Luzon. Governed by village councils of elders and traditional warrior chieftains, the highland society developed advanced mountain rice terrace irrigation and exploited rich upland gold deposits. The mountain federation stubbornly repulsed early lowland Spanish incursions, preserving its indigenous animist customs, communal governance and social independence well beyond the initial conquest of the coastal plains. \n\n Status: Sovereign tribal confederacy; Administrative seat: Sagada; Common languages: Northern Luzon languages; Religion: Traditional animism; Government: Tribal council and chieftaincy; Historical era: Precolonial Philippines; Established: c. 1500; Disestablished: 1576; Historical region: Cordillera Central

name: Ilesa
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: Ilesa was a powerful Yoruba kingdom situated in south-western Nigeria, serving as the metropolitan heart of the Ijesha people. Ruled by a sacred monarch bearing the ancient title of Owa Obokun, the state derived substantial military prowess and commercial wealth from rich agricultural hinterlands and artisanal metalworking. The kingdom remained a dominant regional power throughout the Kiriji War until British colonial mediation and subsequent military treaties brought the territory under the Lagos protectorate in 1891. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ilesa; Common languages: Yoruba; Religion: Traditional Yoruba religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Owa Obokun; Historical era: Early modern Africa; Established: c. 1300; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: British Lagos Protectorate

name: Jajarkot
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: Jajarkot was a sovereign hill principality nestled within the Karnali river basin of western Nepal. As an influential member of the Chaubisi Rajya confederation ruled by the Khas Rajput nobility, the kingdom maintained independent statecraft, levied trans-Himalayan customs dues and sustained local territorial garrisons. Its separate sovereignty ended in 1787 when diplomatic accords and martial pressure incorporated the principality into the rapidly unifying Gorkha Empire under the Shah dynasty. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Jajarkot; Common languages: Nepali and Khas; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Historical era: Early modern South Asia; Established: c. 1500; Disestablished: 1787; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal

name: Ketu
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: Ketu was a venerable Yoruba kingdom established along the borderlands of modern Benin and south-western Nigeria. Governed by a divine sovereign styled the Alaketu, the kingdom claimed direct descent from the royal house of Ile-Ife and maintained extensive fortified settlements surrounded by deep defensive ditches. It preserved its cultural and territorial independence against regional rivals for centuries before suffering devastating raids from Dahomey and eventual administrative partitioning by French and British colonial authorities. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Ketou; Common languages: Yoruba; Religion: Traditional Yoruba religion; Government: Divine monarchy; Ruler title: Alaketu; Historical era: Early modern Africa; Established: c. 1500; Disestablished: 1887; Succeeded by: French Dahomey

name: Khanate of Bukhara
description: The Khanate of Bukhara was a premier Uzbek realm founded in Transoxiana by Muhammad Shaybani following the collapse of the Timurid Empire. The state developed into a preeminent Islamic scholastic and mercantile crossroads along the Silk Road, prospering under the Shaybanid and Janid dynasties. Though temporarily subdued by the Iranian conqueror Nader Shah in 1740, the state regained independence until the non-Chinggisid Manghit ataliqs transformed the realm into the Emirate of Bukhara in the 1780s. \n\n Status: Sovereign khanate; Capital: Bukhara; Common languages: Persian and Chagatai Turkic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Shaybanid and Janid dynasties; Historical era: Early modern Central Asia; Established: 1500; Succeeded by: Emirate of Bukhara

name: Kingdom of Bhurshut
description: The Kingdom of Bhurshut was a traditional Bengali Hindu monarchy spread across the lower Damodar River basin in West Bengal. Ruled by Brahmin monarchs known as the Bhurshut Rajas, the realm flourished as an important centre of Sanskrit learning, Tantric scholarship and riverine agricultural commerce. It retained significant autonomy through cautious diplomacy with the Mughal governors of Bengal until internal family dissension and military expansion by the neighbouring Bardhaman Raj annexed the kingdom in 1713. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Garh Bhawanipur; Common languages: Bengali and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Early modern India; Established: c. 15th century; Disestablished: 1713; Succeeded by: Bardhaman Raj

name: Kingdom of Busoga
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Busoga was a confederated monarchical state situated east of the Victoria Nile in the African Great Lakes region. Composed of eleven hereditary principalities under the supreme cultural and political leadership of the Kyabazinga, the realm prospered through fertile lacustrine farming and regional canoe trade. The kingdom preserved its autonomy against neighbouring Bunyoro and Buganda until the British colonial administration established the Uganda Protectorate and signed formal treaty arrangements in 1901. \n\n Status: Sovereign confederated kingdom; Administrative seat: Jinja; Common languages: Lusoga; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Elective confederate monarchy; Ruler title: Kyabazinga; Historical era: Early modern Africa; Established: c. 1500; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: Uganda Protectorate

name: Kingdom of Daura
description: The Kingdom of Daura was an ancient realm in northern Nigeria celebrated as the spiritual cradle of the Hausa people. Governed by monarchs tracing their royal lineage to the legendary hero Bayajidda and Queen Daurama, the kingdom operated as a vital trans-Saharan trading post and cultural hub. It maintained its sovereign traditions and Islamic institutions until the early nineteenth century, when the expanding Fulani jihad led by Usman dan Fodio conquered the capital in 1806. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Daura; Common languages: Hausa; Religion: Islam and Hausa animism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Sarkin Daura; Historical era: Early modern Africa; Established: c. 10th century; Disestablished: 1806; Succeeded by: Daura Emirate

name: Kingdom of Fazughli
description: The Kingdom of Fazughli was an autonomous riverine realm established in the rugged highlands along the Blue Nile near the modern border of Sudan and Ethiopia. Founded according to regional traditions by Christian refugees following the fall of the Nubian kingdom of Alodia, the state served as a crucial geopolitical buffer between the Funj Sultanate and the Ethiopian Empire. It preserved its cultural distinctiveness and local trade revenues until Sennar annexed the mountain realm in 1685. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Famaka; Common languages: Nubian and Eastern Sudanic languages; Religion: Coptic Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Early modern Africa; Established: c. 1500; Disestablished: 1686; Preceded by: Alodia; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Sennar

name: Kingdom of Gisaka
label: african great lakes kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Gisaka was a powerful Bantu monarchy that flourished in the savannahs and fertile valleys of eastern Rwanda. Ruled by the Gesera dynasty, the state commanded formidable military regiments, managed vast herds of cattle and long rivalled the centralising Nyiginya dynasty of Rwanda for regional supremacy. Dynastic civil wars and territorial fragmentation gradually weakened the realm during the early nineteenth century, culminating in its definitive conquest and incorporation by King Rwabugiri in 1855. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Gisaka; Common languages: Kinyarwanda; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Gesera; Historical era: Early modern Africa; Established: c. 1500; Disestablished: 1855; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Rwanda

name: Kingdom of Ife
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Ife was an ancient Yoruba city-state in south-western Nigeria revered as the mythical and spiritual homeland of the Yoruba civilisation. Governed by the divine Ooni of Ife, the realm exercised immense cultural prestige across the region while preserving renowned traditions of bronze casting, stone carving and terracotta sculpture. The kingdom maintained sovereign autonomy through complex diplomatic balances with larger martial neighbours like Oyo until British colonial authority was established over Yorubaland in 1901. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state kingdom; Capital: Ife; Common languages: Yoruba; Religion: Traditional Yoruba religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Ooni of Ife; Historical era: Early modern Africa; Established: c. 11th century; Disestablished: 1901; Succeeded by: Southern Nigeria Protectorate

name: Kingdom of Janjero
label: kingdoms in the gibe region
description: The Kingdom of Janjero was an isolated mountain monarchy established in the rugged highlands between the Omo and Jimma Gibe Rivers in south-western Ethiopia. Inhabited by the Yem people and ruled by divine kings, the state preserved unique cultural customs, elaborate religious rituals and strong mountain border fortifications against regional expansionists. Its long centuries of independent survival came to an end in 1894 when the imperial armies of Menelik II conquered the kingdom and integrated it into the Ethiopian Empire. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Fofa; Common languages: Yemsa; Religion: Traditional animism and Christianity; Government: Divine monarchy; Historical era: Early modern Africa; Established: c. 15th century; Disestablished: 1895; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Kingdom of Lunda
description: The Kingdom of Lunda was an expansive Central African confederation centred in the fertile savannahs of Katanga. Ruled by a supreme emperor styled the Mwaant Yaav, the realm utilised sophisticated positional succession systems and royal tributary networks to govern diverse communities across present-day Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia. The empire dominated regional ivory and copper trade until internal succession conflicts and aggressive mercantile incursions by Chokwe warlords dismantled its authority in late 1885. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Musumba; Common languages: Chilunda; Religion: Traditional African religion; Government: Confederated monarchy; Ruler title: Mwaant Yaav; Historical era: Early modern Africa; Established: c. 16th century; Disestablished: 1 November 1885; Succeeded by: Chokwe Kingdom

name: Kingdom of Ngoyo
description: The Kingdom of Ngoyo was a coastal Bantu state founded by the Woyo people along the Atlantic littoral just north of the Congo River. Governed by sacred monarchs styled the nfumu nsi, the realm grew prosperous through maritime commerce, deep-sea fishing and active mercantile exchanges with European traders at the port of Cabinda. Political instability and financial exhaustion surrounding the royal enthronement rites weakened the monarchy, which formally dissolved prior to the Portuguese annexation ratified by treaty in 1885. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Cabinda; Common languages: Iwoyo and Kikongo; Religion: Bakongo religion; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Nfumu nsi; Historical era: Early modern Africa; Established: c. 15th century; Disestablished: 1 February 1885; Succeeded by: Portuguese Congo

name: Kingdom of Rwanda
description: The Kingdom of Rwanda was a highly centralised Great Lakes monarchy governed by the sacred mwami of the Nyiginya dynasty. Commanded from royal capitals including Nyanza, the state developed sophisticated pastoral military institutions and expansive territorial administration across the fertile rift valley highlands. After experiencing periods of German and Belgian imperial oversight, the kingdom briefly restored domestic autonomy before ethnic upheaval and the republican referendum of 1961 abolished the monarchy upon full independence in 1962. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Nyanza; Common languages: Kinyarwanda; Religion: Traditional African religion and Roman Catholicism; Government: Centralised monarchy; Ruler title: Mwami; Historical era: Early modern to Contemporary; Established: c. 15th century; Disestablished: 1 July 1962; Succeeded by: First Rwandese Republic

name: Kingdom of Taytay
label: barangay states
description: The Kingdom of Taytay was an autonomous maritime principality centred in northern Palawan in the western Philippine archipelago. Governed by indigenous datus, the coastal polity controlled sheltered bays, maintained vital barter exchanges with visiting Chinese and Bornean merchants and collected forest resins and marine products. It defended its territorial independence against regional corsairs until Spanish monastic expeditions and colonial military garrisons established formal control over northern Palawan during the 1620s. \n\n Status: Sovereign barangay state; Capital: Taytay; Common languages: Cuyonon and Tagbanwa; Religion: Indigenous animism; Government: Chieftaincy; Historical era: Precolonial Philippines; Established: c. 1500; Disestablished: 1624; Succeeded by: Spanish East Indies

name: Kingdom of Vungu
description: The Kingdom of Vungu was a venerable Bantu state located in the forested Mayombe region north of the lower Congo River. Celebrated in oral tradition as a ancestral cradle of the royal lineage that later founded the Kingdom of Kongo, the polity commanded regional trade trails and iron production centres. It sustained localised autonomy alongside kindred northern chieftaincies until advancing administrative consolidation by the kings of Kongo absorbed its remaining territories during the early sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Vungu; Common languages: Kikongo; Religion: Traditional Bakongo religion; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Early modern Africa; Established: c. 13th century; Disestablished: 1536; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Kongo

name: Kingdom of Warri
description: The Kingdom of Warri was a prominent coastal state established by the Itsekiri people in the western Niger Delta. Ruled by the Olu of Warri from his royal seat at Ode-Itsekiri, the kingdom prospered through intensive mercantile contacts with Portuguese, Dutch and British traders who purchased salt, palm oil and textiles. The state retained its political independence and maritime hegemony until intensifying British commercial penetration culminated in a colonial protectorate treaty in 1885. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Warri; Common languages: Itsekiri and Edo; Religion: Traditional religion and Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Olu of Warri; Historical era: Early modern Africa; Established: 1480; Disestablished: 1885; Succeeded by: Oil Rivers Protectorate

name: Kwararafa Confederacy
label: hausa states
description: The Kwararafa Confederacy was a powerful multiethnic empire centred along the Benue River valley in central Nigeria. Directed by sacred monarchs known as the Aku Uka and traditionally associated with the Jukun people, the confederacy mobilised potent cavalry forces that raided far north into Hausaland and Bornu during the seventeenth century.
