description: The Confederation of Sultanates in Lanao was an aristocratic alliance of four Maranao states clustered around Lake Lanao on the inland plateau of Mindanao. Known collectively as the Pat a Pangampong sa Ranao, the member realms preserved communal solidarity through customary laws and shared Islamic jurisprudence. Operating with remarkable local autonomy, the confederacy successfully resisted early Spanish expeditions across the Philippine highlands while maintaining commercial ties with neighbouring Muslim polities. \n\n Status: Confederal sultanate; Capital: Tugaya; Common languages: Maranao, Iranun and Maguindanaon; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Confederated monarchy; Legislature: Council of Elders; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1521; Disestablished: 1641; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Maguindanao

name: Panama
description: Panama during this extensive three-century phase operated partly as a specialised Genoese commercial concession and financial enclave on the Central American isthmus. Backed by wealthy Ligurian merchant syndicates and financiers from the Republic of Genoa, the port connected Pacific silver trade routes with Caribbean galleon fleets under Spanish imperial licensing. The leased trading enclave retained distinct fiscal and maritime privileges until the dissolution of Spanish rule in Central America in 1822. \n\n Status: Commercial leasehold; Capital: Panama City; Common languages: Spanish, Ligurian and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Leased commercial administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1521; Disestablished: 1822; Succeeded by: Gran Colombia

name: Portuguese Timor
description: Portuguese Timor was an overseas colonial territory occupying the eastern half of the island of Timor along with the Oecusse enclave. Originating from early sixteenth-century trading stations and Dominican missions drawn by valuable sandalwood groves, the administration was initially directed from Lifau before moving to Dili in 1769. The colonial authorities governed largely through alliances with indigenous liurai chieftains, enduring Dutch rivalry and twentieth-century wartime turmoil until unilateral decolonisation in November 1975. \n\n Status: Overseas colony; Capital: Dili; Common languages: Portuguese and Tetum; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Ruler title: King of Portugal; Representative title: Governor; Historical era: Early modern to contemporary; Established: 1521; Disestablished: 28 November 1975; Succeeded by: Democratic Republic of East Timor

name: Purépecha Kingdom
label: mesoamerican polities
description: The Purépecha Kingdom was a powerful Mesoamerican state centred around Lake Pátzcuaro in the highlands of modern Michoacán. Governed by the monarch known as the cazonci from his royal court at Tzintzuntzan, the realm maintained a sophisticated tributary network and formidable bronze-equipped armies that had successfully repelled Aztec invasions. Following Spanish contact, the kingdom preserved uneasy autonomy under Tangáxuan II until the conquistadors deposed the monarchy and incorporated the territory into New Spain in 1531. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Tzintzuntzan; Common languages: Purépecha; Religion: Polytheism; Government: Divine absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Vacúxecha; Ruler title: Cazonci; Historical era: Pre-Columbian to early modern; Established: 1521; Disestablished: 1531; Succeeded by: New Spain

name: Solor
description: Solor was a Portuguese colonial trading settlement and missionary stronghold established in the Solor Archipelago east of Flores. Centred around a fortified Dominican monastic outpost, the colony functioned as a crucial transshipment point for sandalwood gathered across the neighbouring Lesser Sunda Islands. Portuguese merchants and friars held the island against repeated assaults by local Muslim rulers and Dutch fleets until the Dutch East India Company captured the fort in the early seventeenth century. \n\n Status: Colonial trading settlement; Capital: Solor; Common languages: Portuguese and Lamaholot; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial military captaincy; Ruler title: King of Portugal; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1521; Disestablished: 1601; Succeeded by: Dutch East India Company

name: Bahrain
description: Bahrain was an insular Gulf dependency seized and fortified by the Portuguese Empire to command maritime trade and the rich pearl beds of the Persian Gulf. Administered from garrisons at Qal'at al-Bahrain and Manama, the colonial authorities extracted customs duties from passing dhows and maintained a tenuous hold over the archipelago's Arab population. Although constantly contested by regional rulers and Ottoman naval squadrons, Portuguese authority persisted until Safavid and tribal forces challenged Lusitanian supremacy. \n\n Status: Colonial dependency; Capital: Manama; Common languages: Arabic and Portuguese; Religion: Sunni Islam, Shia Islam and Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial military governorship; Ruler title: King of Portugal; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1522; Disestablished: 1561; Succeeded by: Safavid Empire

name: Djerba
label: european enclaves in north africa before 1830
description: Djerba was a strategic Spanish insular outpost established in the Gulf of Gabès off the southern coast of modern Tunisia. Operating from the coastal stronghold of Houmt Souk and the Borj El Kebir fortress, the garrison sought to suppress Ottoman corsair operations led by figures such as Dragut. Spanish control proved precarious and temporary, collapsing after devastating Ottoman naval victories in the surrounding waters that forced the evacuation of imperial troops. \n\n Status: Military presidio; Capital: Houmt Souk; Common languages: Spanish, Arabic and Berber; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military governorship; Ruler title: King of Spain; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1522; Disestablished: 1561; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Kingdom of Raigama
description: The Kingdom of Raigama was a short-lived Sinhalese realm created in 1522 in southwestern Sri Lanka during the tripartite partition of the Kingdom of Kotte. Ruled by Prince Raigam Bandara from his seat near Bandaragama, the polity governed fertile inland territories while maintaining a delicate balance between rival brother kingdoms. Following the demise of its sole monarch in 1539, the kingdom was quickly absorbed by the neighbouring Kingdom of Sitawaka under Mayadunne. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bandaragama; Common languages: Sinhala; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Transitional period; Established: 1522; Disestablished: 1539; Preceded by: Kingdom of Kotte; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sitawaka

name: Kingdom of Sitawaka
description: The Kingdom of Sitawaka was a powerful Sinhalese state established in the south-central interior of Sri Lanka after the division of Kotte. Under energetic sovereigns Mayadunne and Rajasinha I, the kingdom rapidly expanded across the lowlands and mounted fierce military campaigns against Portuguese enclaves in Colombo. Despite its martial brilliance and dominance over interior trade, the realm crumbled following succession disputes and battlefield setbacks after the death of Rajasinha I in the 1590s. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Sitawaka; Common languages: Sinhala; Religion: Theravada Buddhism and Shaivism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Transitional period; Established: 1522; Disestablished: 1594; Preceded by: Kingdom of Kotte; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Kandy and Portuguese Ceylon

name: Muharraq
description: Muharraq functioned as a fortified Portuguese maritime outpost located on the island immediately northeast of Bahrain's main landmass. The settlement served as a vital naval anchorage and collection point for the Persian Gulf's prized natural pearl fisheries. Portuguese garrisons maintained defensive watchtowers over the shallow waters to safeguard shipping against Arabian raiders until imperial military presence across the archipelago waned in the mid-sixteenth century. \n\n Status: Colonial port dependency; Capital: Muharraq; Common languages: Portuguese and Arabic; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Sunni Islam; Government: Naval military station; Ruler title: King of Portugal; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1522; Disestablished: 1561; Succeeded by: Safavid Empire

name: Qatar
description: Qatar in the early sixteenth century became a coastal dependency under Portuguese maritime hegemony along the northeastern shores of the Arabian Peninsula. Based out of the coastal settlement at Al Huwaylah, Portuguese naval commanders supervised maritime trade and secured transit routes across the southern Persian Gulf. The outpost faced persistent hostility from local Bedouin tribes and rising Ottoman naval squadrons, leading to Lisbon's eventual abandonment of the peninsula by 1551. \n\n Status: Colonial trading station; Capital: Al Huwaylah; Common languages: Portuguese and Arabic; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Sunni Islam; Government: Military captaincy; Ruler title: King of Portugal; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1522; Disestablished: 1551; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Samudera Pasai Sultanate
description: The Samudera Pasai Sultanate in this brief terminal phase existed as a Portuguese colonial garrison state on the northern coast of Sumatra. Following the Portuguese expeditionary capture of the ancient trading port in 1521, imperial troops occupied the capital to monopolise regional pepper exports and dominate the Malacca Strait. Relentless assaults from the neighbouring Sultanate of Aceh made the European position untenable, forcing the Portuguese garrison to evacuate before Aceh formally annexed the territory. \n\n Status: Colonial occupied territory; Capital: Pasai; Common languages: Portuguese and Old Malay; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Sunni Islam; Government: Military occupation government; Ruler title: King of Portugal; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1522; Disestablished: 1525; Succeeded by: Aceh Sultanate

name: Spanish East Indies
description: The Spanish East Indies formed a vast overseas colonial domain encompassing the Philippine archipelago, Guam, the Mariana Islands and the Caroline Islands. Governed through the Captaincy General from the fortified city of Manila, the colony served as the western terminus of the historic Manila Galleon trade that linked Asian markets with New Spain. The territory remained under Spanish imperial sovereignty for over three centuries until American naval forces seized Manila during the Spanish-American War in August 1898. \n\n Status: Overseas territory of the Spanish Empire; Capital: Manila; Official languages: Spanish; Common languages: Tagalog, Ilocano, Cebuano and Chamorro; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Captaincy general; Ruler title: King of Spain; Representative title: Governor-General; Historical era: Early modern to modern; Established: 1522; Disestablished: 13 August 1898; Succeeded by: United States Military Government of the Philippine Islands

name: United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg
label: holy roman empire
description: The United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg was a powerful composite principality of the Holy Roman Empire spanning the lower Rhine and Westphalia. Formed through dynastic union and administered from Düsseldorf, the realm encompassed the duchies of Jülich, Cleves and Berg alongside the counties of Mark and Ravensberg. The state pursued moderate religious policies amidst surrounding confessional turbulence until the extinction of its ruling ducal dynasty in 1609 provoked a contentious European succession crisis. \n\n Status: Composite duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Düsseldorf; Common languages: German, Kleverlandish, Ripuarian and Westphalian; Religion: Roman Catholicism, Lutheranism and Calvinism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of La Marck; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1522; Disestablished: 1 May 1609; Succeeded by: Margraviate of Brandenburg and Palatinate-Neuburg

name: Peñón de Vélez de la Gomera
label: berber kingdoms
description: Peñón de Vélez de la Gomera functioned as a Moroccan coastal stronghold and naval base located off the rocky Rif shoreline opposite Badis. Captured from a Spanish garrison in late 1522 by Wattasid-aligned Berber forces, the tied island protected regional corsair anchorages and maritime trade routes across the western Mediterranean. The fortification remained an active Moroccan bastion against European maritime incursions for over three decades before being ceded into the Ottoman sphere in the 1550s. \n\n Status: Fortified island stronghold; Capital: Badis; Common languages: Berber and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Feudal military governorship; Ruling dynasty: Wattasid dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan of Morocco; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 20 December 1522; Disestablished: 1555; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Maluku
description: Maluku during this period constituted a Portuguese colonial network of trading stations and fortified redoubts in the Spice Islands of eastern Indonesia. Operating primarily from bases on Ambon, Ternate and Tidore, Portuguese captains strove to dominate international commerce in cloves, nutmeg and mace. Intense rivalries with local sultanates and persistent conflict with Spanish and native forces steadily undermined the colony until Dutch East India Company fleets displaced the Portuguese in the early seventeenth century. \n\n Status: Colonial trading domain; Capital: Ambon; Common languages: Portuguese, Malay and Ambonese; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Sunni Islam; Government: Captaincy general; Ruler title: King of Portugal; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1523; Disestablished: 1606; Succeeded by: Dutch East India Company

name: Duchy of Pomerania-Stettin
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Pomerania-Stettin during this interim era was a Baltic feudal principality held in vassalage to the Electorate of Brandenburg within the Holy Roman Empire. Governed by the Griffin dynasty from the port city of Szczecin, the realm controlled fertile agricultural lowlands and valuable commercial avenues along the lower Oder River. Brandenburgian feudal suzerainty caused enduring friction until the Treaty of Grimnitz in August 1529 restored the duchy to imperial immediacy with mutual succession agreements. \n\n Status: Vassal duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Szczecin; Common languages: Low German and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Griffin dynasty; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1524; Disestablished: 26 August 1529; Succeeded by: Duchy of Pomerania-Stettin

name: Duchy of Pomerania-Wolgast
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Pomerania-Wolgast was a coastal feudal realm in Western Pomerania subjected to Brandenburgian suzerainty following dynastic divisions among the Griffin dukes. Ruling from the fortified ducal residence at Wolgast, the administration oversaw maritime communities and agrarian estates along the Peene River and the Baltic coastline. The contentious feudal subordination to the Hohenzollern electors of Brandenburg formally concluded on 26 August 1529 when the Treaty of Grimnitz granted Pomerania direct imperial immediacy. \n\n Status: Vassal duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Wolgast; Common languages: Low German and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Griffin dynasty; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1524; Disestablished: 26 August 1529; Succeeded by: Duchy of Pomerania-Wolgast

name: Kaqchikel Kingdom
description: The Kaqchikel Kingdom in this brief four-month phase existed as a Highland Maya client state allied to the Spanish conquistadors under Pedro de Alvarado. Centred at the fortified capital of Iximche, the Kaqchikel leadership initially collaborated with the Spaniards to defeat their traditional rivals, the neighbouring K'iche' Maya. Severe Spanish extortion, demands for gold tribute and oppressive mistreatment rapidly alienated the indigenous rulers, provoking a general uprising on 28 August 1524 that initiated years of guerrilla warfare. \n\n Status: Vassal indigenous kingdom; Capital: Iximche; Common languages: Kaqchikel and Spanish; Religion: Maya religion; Government: Traditional indigenous monarchy; Ruler title: Ajpo Tz'ok; Historical era: Spanish conquest; Established: 14 April 1524; Disestablished: 28 August 1524; Succeeded by: Kaqchikel Kingdom

name: Kaqchikel Kingdom
description: The Kaqchikel Kingdom during this six-year phase was an independent Highland Maya resistance state fighting for survival against Spanish colonial encroachment. Abandoning their capital at Iximche following their revolt in August 1524, Kaqchikel warriors under Ahpozotzil Kaji Imox waged persistent guerrilla warfare from mountain forests and fortified highland hideouts. Overwhelming Spanish firepower and continuous campaigns eventually broke organised resistance, forcing the royal leadership to surrender formally on 9 May 1530. \n\n Status: Independent indigenous kingdom; Capital: Iximche; Common languages: Kaqchikel; Religion: Maya religion; Government: Traditional indigenous monarchy; Ruler title: Ajpo Tz'ok; Historical era: Spanish conquest; Established: 28 August 1524; Disestablished: 9 May 1530; Succeeded by: Captaincy General of Guatemala

name: Baria State
description: Baria State was a prominent Rajput principality located within the hilly forests of eastern Gujarat in the Rewa Kantha region. Founded in 1525 by descendants of the Khichi Chauhan dynasty, the kingdom governed around its fortified capital at Devgadh Baria amidst rugged terrain. The rulers maintained political autonomy through shifting alliances with regional powers and local Bhil chieftains until British paramountcy restructured the princely state system in the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Devgadh Baria; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Khichi Chauhan Rajput; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1525; Disestablished: 1865; Succeeded by: Baria State (British protectorate)

name: Duchy of Prussia
description: The Duchy of Prussia was a Protestant feudal state established in eastern Prussia following the secularisation of the Monastic State of the Teutonic Knights in April 1525. Ruled by Duke Albert of Hohenzollern from Königsberg, the realm became the world's first officially Lutheran polity while acknowledging the feudal suzerainty of the Polish crown. The duchy developed flourishing maritime trade and scholarship until dynastic inheritance merged the territory into a personal union with the Margraviate of Brandenburg in 1619. \n\n Status: Feudal duchy under Polish suzerainty; Capital: Königsberg; Common languages: German, Low German, Polish, Lithuanian and Old Prussian; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Hohenzollern; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Protestant Reformation; Established: 8 April 1525; Disestablished: 1619; Succeeded by: Brandenburg-Prussia

name: Kasur
description: Kasur was an autonomous Afghan principality established in the central Punjab south of Lahore during the political fragmentation following the fall of the Delhi Sultanate. Settled and fortified by Kheshgi Pashtun clans, the state comprised an aggregation of defensive hamlets overlooking the fertile alluvial valleys of the Sutlej and Beas rivers. The local leaders retained independent commercial and military authority until the expanding Mughal administration under Akbar integrated the Punjab into imperial provincial rule. \n\n Status: City-state principality; Capital: Kasur; Common languages: Punjabi, Pashto and Persian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Aristocratic tribal chieftaincy; Ruling dynasty: Kheshgi clan; Ruler title: Nawab; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1526; Disestablished: 1551; Succeeded by: Mughal Empire

name: Mughal Empire
description: The Mughal Empire was a premier early modern imperial state founded in northern India by Babur following his decisive victory at the First Battle of Panipat in April 1526. From historic capitals at Agra, Delhi and Lahore, the Timurid dynasty established sophisticated centralised institutions, patronised splendid Persianate arts and commanded vast agrarian revenues. Although briefly displaced by the Afghan Sur dynasty in 1540, the empire was subsequently restored and expanded across virtually the entire Indian subcontinent. \n\n Status: Empire; Capital: Agra; Official languages: Persian; Common languages: Hindustani, Persian and Chagatai Turkic; Religion: Sunni Islam and Hinduism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Mughal dynasty; Ruler title: Padishah; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 21 April 1526; Disestablished: 17 May 1540; Succeeded by: Sur Empire

name: Duchy of Milan (Military Occupation)
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Milan in this turbulent phase was an imperial territory held under direct Austrian Habsburg military occupation during the War of the League of Cognac. Stationed across the Lombard plain, imperial garrisons governed through emergency martial decrees to counter French and Papal forces seeking to control northern Italy. The occupation maintained stringent fiscal exactions and garrisons until imperial diplomacy restored Duke Francesco II Sforza to nominal authority under the Treaty of Cambrai. \n\n Status: Territory under military occupation; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Lombard and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Imperial military administration; Ruler title: Holy Roman Emperor; Historical era: Italian Wars; Established: 10 July 1526; Disestablished: 1530; Succeeded by: Duchy of Milan

name: Sultanate of Banjar
description: The Sultanate of Banjar was a prominent maritime Islamic monarchy established in south-eastern Borneo following the conversion of King Surianshah in September 1526. Centred in the Barito River basin and later administered from Martapura, the sultanate commanded regional commerce in pepper, gold and forest products across the Java Sea. The realm fiercely guarded its sovereignty against rival regional sultanates and early Dutch mercantilist overtures before expanding its inland riverine trade networks. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Martapura; Official languages: Banjar; Common languages: Banjar, Malay and Dayak languages; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Banjar dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 24 September 1526; Disestablished: 1788; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Banjar (Dutch protectorate)

name: Serb Empire of Jovan Nenad
description: The Serb Empire of Jovan Nenad was a short-lived insurrectionary state founded in the southern Pannonian Plain in the chaotic aftermath of the Battle of Mohács. Led by the charismatic military commander Jovan Nenad, known as the Black, the regime cleared Ottoman forces from Bačka, Banat and parts of Syrmia while establishing its headquarters at Subotica. Styling himself Tsar of the Serbs, Nenad mobilised regional Orthodox fighters until he was defeated and killed by Hungarian aristocratic forces in July 1527. \n\n Status: Insurrectionary monarchy; Capital: Subotica; Common languages: Serbian and Hungarian; Religion: Serbian Orthodoxy; Government: Military monarchy; Ruler title: Tsar; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 October 1526; Disestablished: 26 July 1527; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Hungary

name: Kingdom of Hungary
description: The Kingdom of Hungary during this fractured transitional phase comprised the independent realm governed by King John Zápolya in the eastern lands of Hungary and Transylvania. Elected monarch by the national nobility after the catastrophic defeat at Mohács, Zápolya established his administrative seat at Alba Iulia and contested Habsburg claims to the Hungarian crown. Faced with imperial Austrian military pressure, Zápolya ruled autonomously until escalating warfare forced him to enter into a tributary alliance with the Ottoman Empire in 1530. \n\n Status: Contested kingdom; Capital: Alba Iulia; Common languages: Hungarian, Latin and Romanian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Zápolya; Ruler title: King of Hungary; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 November 1526; Disestablished: 1530; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Hungary (Ottoman vassal)

name: Kingdom of Ava
description: The Kingdom of Ava in this subordinate era functioned as a puppet state in Upper Burma dominated by the Confederation of Shan States. Following the violent sack of the city in March 1527 by Sawlon of Mohnyin, Avan princes held nominal authority while Shan overlords exercised effective political and military governance. The regime contended with fierce domestic resentment, ethnic discord and chronic instability until the expanding Toungoo Dynasty under King Bayinnaung captured Inwa in January 1555. \n\n Status: Puppet kingdom; Capital: Inwa; Common languages: Burmese and Shan; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Monarchy under foreign military control; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 15 March 1527; Disestablished: 22 January 1555; Succeeded by: Toungoo Dynasty

name: Shan States Confederation
label: shan states
description: The Shan States Confederation was a formidable military alliance of Tai-Shan principalities, including Mohnyin, Mogaung, Bhamo and Kale, that came together in northern Burma. Spearheaded by Sawlon of Mohnyin, the confederation conquered the central Irrawaddy heartland in March 1527, establishing its administrative dominance from the seat of Ava. The allied saophas ruled extensive territories across Upper Burma for nearly three decades before internal divisions and the military ascendancy of the Toungoo Empire fractured their collective authority. \n\n Status: Confederal monarchy; Capital: Ava; Common languages: Shan and Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism and traditional animism; Government: Confederal monarchy; Ruler title: Saopha; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 15 March 1527; Disestablished: 1556; Succeeded by: Toungoo Dynasty

name: Holy Roman Empire and Kingdom of Spain (Military Occupation)
description: The Holy Roman Empire and Kingdom of Spain Military Occupation comprised the nine-month joint Habsburg martial administration imposed over central Italy following the catastrophic Sack of Rome on 6 May 1527. Imperial and Spanish regiments seized the pontifical capital, plundered religious archives and besieged Pope Clement VII inside the Castel Sant'Angelo. Operating without a civil administrative centre, the mutinous occupational command dictated political terms until disease, supply shortages and diplomatic negotiations compelled imperial forces to withdraw in February 1528. \n\n Status: Joint military occupation zone; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Spanish, German, Latin and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Wartime military administration; Ruler title: Holy Roman Emperor; Historical era: Italian Wars; Established: 6 May 1527; Disestablished: 17 February 1528; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Republic of Florence
label: holy roman empire
description: The Republic of Florence during this dramatic final phase was a revived republican commonwealth proclaimed after the citizens expelled the Medici family in May 1527. Governed by the restored Signoria and the Great Council, the republic reinstated communal civic liberties and prepared comprehensive fortifications supervised by Michelangelo. Florence's republican independence ended tragically on 12 August 1530 after a brutal ten-month siege by allied Imperial and Papal forces, leading directly to the establishment of the hereditary Medici duchy. \n\n Status: Merchant republic; Capital: Florence; Official languages: Italian and Latin; Common languages: Florentine Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Oligarchic republic; Ruler title: Gonfaloniere di Giustizia; Legislature: Great Council; Historical era: Renaissance; Established: 16 May 1527; Disestablished: 12 August 1530; Succeeded by: Duchy of Florence

name: Duchy of Syrmia
label: serbian principalities
description: The Duchy of Syrmia was an autonomous Serbian borderland domain established in the Syrmian peninsula between the Danube and Sava rivers after the collapse of Jovan Nenad's regime. Governed by Duke Radoslav Čelnik from his fortified seat at Ilok, the principality accepted Ottoman tributary vassalage to protect the local Christian population from devastation. Čelnik maintained a delicate diplomatic balancing act along the contested imperial frontier until shifting regional loyalties prompted him to seek Habsburg protection in 1531. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of the Ottoman Empire; Capital: Ilok; Common languages: Serbian, Hungarian and Ottoman Turkish; Religion: Serbian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal principality; Ruler title: Duke; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 November 1527; Disestablished: 1531; Succeeded by: Duchy of Syrmia (Habsburg vassal)

name: Banswara State
description: Banswara State was a sovereign Rajput principality established in southern Rajasthan across the rugged hill country of Vagad. Founded in 1528 by Maharawal Jagmal Singh of the Sisodia dynasty, the realm established its dynastic seat at Banswara amidst a predominantly Bhil indigenous population. The state vigorously defended its autonomy against neighbouring Mewar and Dungarpur before navigating periodic tributary demands from Mughal and Maratha overlords until signing a subsidiary alliance with the British in November 1818. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Banswara; Common languages: Vagdi, Rajasthani and Mewari; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sisodia dynasty; Ruler title: Maharawal; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1528; Disestablished: 16 November 1818; Succeeded by: Banswara State (British protectorate)

name: Kalinyamat Sultanate
description: The Kalinyamat Sultanate, also known as the Sultanate of Jepara, was a maritime Islamic power established along the northern coast of Central Java. Emerging from the declining Demak Sultanate under the leadership of Queen Kalinyamat and Sultan Hadlirin, the realm developed into a major naval hub and trading centre. Jepara launched ambitious naval expeditions against Portuguese fortresses in Malacca before the kingdom was ultimately conquered by the expanding Mataram Sultanate around 1600. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Jepara; Common languages: Javanese; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1528; Disestablished: 1600; Preceded by: Demak Sultanate; Succeeded by: Mataram Sultanate

name: Kingdom of Sumedang Larang
description: The Kingdom of Sumedang Larang was a Sundanese Islamic state that flourished across the inland plateau of the Parahyangan region in western Java. Established following the disintegration of the Hindu-Buddhist Sunda Kingdom, the realm governed from its royal seat at Kutamaya near modern Sumedang. Its monarchs preserved traditional Sundanese customs while fostering Islamic statecraft, maintaining sovereignty until regional military pressures forced its integration into the Mataram Sultanate in 1621. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Sumedang; Common languages: Sundanese; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: Prabu; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1528; Disestablished: 1621; Preceded by: Sunda Kingdom; Succeeded by: Mataram Sultanate

name: Sultanate of Banten
description: The Sultanate of Banten was an influential Islamic maritime trading power established on the north-western coast of Java along the strategic Sunda Strait. Founded by Sunan Gunungjati and Sultan Maulana Hasanuddin, the state grew into a cosmopolitan commercial metropolis driven by its global monopoly over the regional pepper harvest. Banten conducted diplomacy with European and Asian courts while resisting Dutch mercantile pressure until domestic conflicts enabled the Dutch East India Company to dismantle its independence. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Serang; Common languages: Bantenese, Sundanese and Javanese; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bantenese royal house; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1528; Disestablished: 22 November 1808; Succeeded by: Dutch East Indies

name: Clipperton Island
description: Clipperton Island was an isolated oceanic possession claimed for the Spanish Empire in the eastern Pacific Ocean west of Mexico. Sighted on 15 November 1528 by the navigator Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón, the coral atoll was claimed under imperial maritime decrees as Isla de la Pasión. Devoid of fresh water and permanent inhabitants, the remote ring remained an uncolonised navigational landmark on Pacific charts until French merchant vessels rediscovered the atoll in April 1711. \n\n Status: Uninhabited colonial claim; Capital: None (decentralised); Common languages: Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Unadministered maritime dependency; Ruler title: King of Spain; Historical era: Age of Discovery; Established: 15 November 1528; Disestablished: 3 April 1711; Succeeded by: Kingdom of France

name: Province of Venezuela
description: The Province of Venezuela during this distinctive interlude functioned as an autonomous proprietary colony administered by the German Welser banking family of Augsburg. Granted territorial rights by Emperor Charles V to settle imperial debts, German governors operated from Santa Ana de Coro to mount expeditions inland in search of El Dorado. Mismanagement, lethal conflicts with indigenous populations and mounting friction with Spanish authorities prompted the crown to revoke the Welser concession and reassert direct royal control. \n\n Status: Proprietary colony; Capital: Coro; Common languages: German and Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Chartered commercial governorship; Ruler title: Holy Roman Emperor; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1529; Disestablished: 1545; Succeeded by: Venezuela Province

name: Sultanate of Johor
