name: Tigiria State
description: Tigiria State was a sovereign Hindu principality located in the Mahanadi River basin in present-day Cuttack district, Odisha. Established during the sixteenth century by Raja Nityananda Tunga of the Somavanshi dynasty, it was the smallest yet most densely populated of the Garhjat states of the Orissa highlands. The principality preserved local self-rule and managed tribute relations with surrounding powers until 1802, when British forces established paramount control across coastal Odisha. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Tigiria; Ruling dynasty: Tunga; Common languages: Odia; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Established: 16th century; Disestablished: 1802; Succeeded by: British East India Company

name: Tulsipur State
description: Tulsipur State was a prominent feudatory kingdom spanning the Dang and Deukhuri valleys in the Siwalik hills, extending southward into the fertile Tarai plains of Awadh. Traditionally inhabited by the indigenous Tharu people and ruled by Chauhan Rajput rajas, the realm functioned as one of the Baise Rajya confederated hill states. While its northern Himalayan valley territories were absorbed by Nepal in 1786, the southern domains around Tulsipur maintained autonomy until annexed by the British following the 1857 rebellion. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Tulsipur; Ruling dynasty: Chauhan Rajput; Common languages: Tharu, Awadhi, Nepali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Disestablished: 1860; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal, British Raj

name: Uukwanyama
description: Uukwanyama was a powerful sovereign kingdom of the Ovambo people established in the fertile floodplains of the Cuvelai basin across modern northern Namibia and southern Angola. Ruled by hereditary monarchs titled ohamba from their royal residences at Ondjiva and Oihole, the kingdom maintained formidable military regiments and rich herds of cattle. Uukwanyama fiercely defended its territorial sovereignty against European incursions until the late nineteenth century, resisting Portuguese and German colonial advances until final conquest in the early twentieth century. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Ondjiva; Common languages: Oshikwanyama; Religion: Traditional beliefs; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Ohamba; Historical era: Pre-colonial; Disestablished: 1896; Succeeded by: Portuguese Angola, German South West Africa

name: Kingdom of Kotte
description: The Kingdom of Kotte was an ancient Sinhalese monarchy situated in south-western Sri Lanka that came under Portuguese vassalage during the reign of the baptised King Dom Joao Dharmapala. Operating from Colombo alongside Portuguese garrison forces, the beleaguered court faced relentless military assaults from the rival Sinhalese Kingdom of Sitawaka. Dharmapala bequeathed his royal dominions to King Philip I of Portugal upon his death in 1597, leading directly to the establishment of Portuguese Ceylon. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Portugal; Capital: Colombo; Common languages: Sinhala, Portuguese, Tamil; Religion: Roman Catholicism, Theravada Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Head of state: Dom Joao Dharmapala; Disestablished: 1598; Succeeded by: Portuguese Ceylon

name: Principality of Bayreuth (Military Occupation)
label: holy roman empire
description: The Principality of Bayreuth Military Occupation designated the Franconian and imperial territories held under martial control by Margrave Albert Alcibiades of Brandenburg-Kulmbach during the Second Margrave War. Driven by ambitions to carve out an enlarged Duchy of Franconia, the margrave's forces seized ecclesiastical lands belonging to the bishoprics of Bamberg and Wurzburg alongside neighbouring imperial cities. The occupation collapsed in November 1554 after an imperial coalition defeated Albert's forces and laid siege to his strongholds. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: None (decentralised); Common languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Reformation; Established: 19 May 1552; Disestablished: 1 November 1554; Historical region: Franconia

name: Sultanate of Touggourt
description: The Sultanate of Touggourt was an oasis principality located in the Oued Righ valley of the northern Algerian Sahara, governed by the Berber dynasty of the Banu Djellab. Following an armed expedition led by Salah Rais, the Ottoman Beylerbey of Algiers, the sultanate was compelled in November 1552 to submit to Ottoman suzerainty and pay annual dates tribute. The sultans retained internal autonomy over caravan routes and date palms until centralising French military campaigns dissolved the state in the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Vassal sultanate of the Ottoman Empire; Capital: Touggourt; Ruling dynasty: Banu Djellab; Common languages: Berber, Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Sultanate; Ruler title: Sultan; Established: 1 November 1552; Disestablished: 1813

name: Qasim Khanate
description: The Qasim Khanate was a Tatar principality situated along the middle course of the Oka River in Ryazan, serving as an autonomous protectorate of the Tsardom of Russia. Following the Muscovite conquest of Kazan in 1552, the autonomous political privileges of the reigning Chinggisid khans were curtailed as Russian voyevodas assumed supervisory military administration. The khanate functioned as a vital diplomatic conduit and cavalry auxiliary for Moscow until its formal dissolution upon the death of Khanbika Fatima Soltan in 1681. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Russia; Capital: Kasimov; Ruling dynasty: Chinggisid; Official languages: Old Tatar, Russian; Religion: Sunni Islam, Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Khanate; Ruler title: Khan; Established: 1553; Disestablished: 1682; Succeeded by: Tsardom of Russia

name: Kingdom of Makwanpur
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: The Kingdom of Makwanpur was a sovereign hill state founded by the Sena dynasty across the northern fringes of the Mithila region in central-southern Nepal. Centred on the mountain stronghold of Makwanpurgadhi, the realm controlled key trade arteries and fertile Tarai lowlands, maintaining Maithili as its royal court language. Makwanpur preserved its sovereignty until August 1762, when Prithvi Narayan Shah defeated King Digbandhan Sen in battle and annexed the kingdom into the unified Gorkhali domain. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Makwanpurgadhi; Ruling dynasty: Sena; Official languages: Maithili; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Disestablished: 24 August 1762; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal

name: Alliance of Holy Roman Empire States
label: holy roman empire
description: The Alliance of Holy Roman Empire States, known historically as the Heidelberg League, was a defensive confederation of imperial princes organised during the Second Margrave War. Formed by regional rulers including the Elector of Saxony, the Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbuttel and neighbouring ecclesiastical lords, the alliance sought to curb the aggressive territorial ambitions of Margrave Albert Alcibiades of Brandenburg-Kulmbach. The coalition fielded combined imperial armies, successfully dismantling Albert's garrisons and restoring regional peace across Franconia by 1555. \n\n Status: Defensive confederation; Administrative seat: None (decentralised); Common languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism, Roman Catholicism; Government: Confederation of imperial estates; Historical era: Reformation; Established: 1 July 1554; Disestablished: 1555; Historical region: Franconia

name: Duchy of Holstein-Gottorp
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Holstein-Gottorp was a sovereign principality in northern Germany ruled by a cadet branch of the House of Oldenburg, exercising territorial superiority over portions of Schleswig and Holstein. Headquartered at Gottorf Castle and later Kiel, the dukes asserted imperial immediacy within the Holy Roman Empire while frequently contesting sovereignty with the Danish Crown. The duchy pursued ambitious Baltic alliances, notably with Sweden and Russia, until territorial swaps consolidated ducal claims with Denmark in the eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Kiel; Ruling dynasty: House of Holstein-Gottorp; Common languages: Low German, German, Danish; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Duke of Holstein-Gottorp; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1555

name: Hindol State
description: Hindol State was an independent princely domain established in the forested Garhjat hill tracts of modern-day Dhenkanal district in Odisha. Founded around the mid-sixteenth century by members of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, the principality governed agrarian settlements from its hilltop capital at Hindol. The rulers maintained internal administrative autonomy while navigating shifting tributary pressures from neighbouring Gajapati and Maratha forces until the British East India Company assumed regional paramountcy in 1804. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Hindol; Ruling dynasty: Eastern Ganga; Common languages: Odia; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Established: 1555; Disestablished: 1804; Succeeded by: British East India Company

name: Peñón de Vélez de la Gomera
description: Peñón de Vélez de la Gomera was a heavily fortified tidal islet on the Mediterranean coast of Morocco held by the Ottoman Empire as a forward corsair base. Ceded to Ottoman forces in 1554 by the Wattasid sultan Ali Abu Hassun in exchange for military support, the rocky stronghold harboured Barbary corsairs who raided Christian shipping across the Alboran Sea. Ottoman control ended on 6 September 1564 when a Spanish naval armada under Garcia Alvarez de Toledo recaptured the garrison. \n\n Status: Ottoman naval outpost; Administrative seat: Peñón de Vélez de la Gomera; Common languages: Ottoman Turkish, Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military garrison; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1555; Disestablished: 6 September 1564; Succeeded by: Spanish Empire

name: Tarkhan Dynasty
description: The Tarkhan Dynasty was a sovereign Turco-Mongol ruling house that established control over Sindh in the Indus River delta following the collapse of the Arghun dynasty. Founded by Mirza Isa Beg Tarkhan, the dynasty governed from the prosperous riverine capital of Thatta, repelling Portuguese naval incursions and negotiating division of upper Sindh with local rivals. Sovereign Tarkhan authority concluded in 1592 when Mughal imperial armies under Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan subdued Mirza Jani Beg and incorporated Sindh into Akbar's empire. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Thatta; Ruling dynasty: Tarkhan; Official languages: Persian; Common languages: Sindhi, Persian, Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Mirza; Established: 1555; Disestablished: 1592; Succeeded by: Mughal Empire

name: Kingdom of Imereti
description: The Kingdom of Imereti was a Christian Georgian monarchy in western Transcaucasia ruled by the Bagrationi dynasty from its royal seat at Kutaisi. Under the Peace of Amasya concluded in May 1555 between the Ottoman and Safavid empires, western Georgia fell under the Iranian sphere of tributary vassalage. King Bagrat III and his successors maintained internal ecclesiastical and feudal governance while navigating onerous Safavid tributary demands, until Ottoman military incursions subsequently shifted regional hegemony. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Safavid Empire; Capital: Kutaisi; Ruling dynasty: Bagrationi; Official languages: Georgian; Religion: Georgian Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Established: 29 May 1555; Disestablished: 1 September 1576

name: France Antarctique
description: France Antarctique was an early French colonial settlement established on Guanabara Bay in southeastern Brazil under the leadership of Nicolas Durand de Villegaignon. Designed as a strategic naval base for French maritime commerce and a haven for Huguenots, the colony centred on Fort Coligny on Serigipe Island. Beset by theological disputes and fierce indigenous alliances, the French outpost was assaulted and destroyed on 17 March 1560 by Portuguese colonial forces commanded by Governor-General Mem de Sa. \n\n Status: French colony; Capital: Fort Coligny; Common languages: French, Tupi; Religion: Calvinism, Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Age of Discovery; Established: 1556; Disestablished: 17 March 1560; Succeeded by: Portuguese Brazil

name: Massawa
description: Massawa was a vital Red Sea island port on the coast of present-day Eritrea held temporarily by the Portuguese Empire during their maritime struggle against Ottoman naval expansion. Functioning as a fortified transhipment post and supply staging point for Portuguese diplomatic missions to the Ethiopian Empire, the port facilitated contact with the Christian Solomonic court. Portuguese naval hegemony over the island proved brief, collapsing in 1558 when Ottoman forces under Ozdemir Pasha captured the town and annexed it to the Habesh Eyalet. \n\n Status: Portuguese fortified outpost; Administrative seat: Massawa; Common languages: Portuguese, Tigre, Arabic; Religion: Roman Catholicism, Islam; Government: Military garrison; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1556; Disestablished: 1558; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Spanish Netherlands
label: holy roman empire
description: The Spanish Netherlands encompassed the collection of imperial fiefs in the Low Countries held in personal union by the Spanish branch of the House of Habsburg following the abdication of Emperor Charles V. Governed from Brussels through royal governors-general and protected by the formidable Army of Flanders, the territory formed a vital northern bulwark of the Spanish Empire. Although the northern provinces broke away during the Dutch Revolt, the southern provinces remained staunchly Catholic Spanish possessions until the War of the Spanish Succession. \n\n Status: Spanish Habsburg possession; Capital: Brussels; Ruling dynasty: House of Habsburg; Common languages: Dutch, French, Walloon, Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Governorate; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 16 January 1556; Currency: Patagon, Gulden

name: State of the Presidi
label: holy roman empire
description: The State of the Presidi was a strategically vital enclave of coastal garrisons situated along the Tuscan littoral and the Monte Argentario promontory. Created by King Philip II of Spain following the Treaty of London and the partition of the Republic of Siena, the domain was governed from the citadel of Orbetello by military commanders answerable to the viceroy of Naples. The coastal fortresses served to anchor Spanish maritime communications and oversee central Italian waters throughout the Habsburg era. \n\n Status: Spanish military dependency; Capital: Orbetello; Common languages: Italian, Spanish; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military governorship; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 3 July 1557; Disestablished: 1709; Succeeded by: Austrian Habsburg Monarchy

name: Livonian Confederation
label: states emerged from the northern crusades
description: The Livonian Confederation was a late medieval ecclesiastical league in present-day Estonia and Latvia, comprising the Livonian Order and four prince-bishoprics. Under mounting threat from Muscovite expansionism, the confederation concluded the Treaty of Pozvol on 14 September 1557, accepting military protection from King Sigismund II Augustus of Poland-Lithuania. The protectorate failed to halt catastrophic Russian invasions during the Livonian War, culminating on 28 November 1561 in the Treaty of Vilnius, which dissolved the confederation and partitioned its Baltic lands. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Poland-Lithuania; Capital: Riga; Common languages: Middle Low German, Latin, Estonian, Latvian; Religion: Roman Catholicism, Lutheranism; Government: Theocratic confederation; Legislature: Livonian Landtag; Established: 14 September 1557; Disestablished: 28 November 1561

name: Hsenwi State
label: shan states
description: Hsenwi State was a premier Shan principality situated in the rugged highlands of northern Burma along the upper Salween River basin. Following the sweeping military campaigns of King Bayinnaung of the Toungoo dynasty, the hereditary saopha of Hsenwi submitted to Burmese royal suzerainty in 1558. Governed from its capital at Theinni, the state provided royal levies and tribute to the Burmese court while retaining substantial autonomy over its multi-ethnic hill population until British colonial annexation in 1886. \n\n Status: Vassal Shan state of Burma; Capital: Hsenwi; Common languages: Shan, Tai Nuea, Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Saopha; Established: 1558; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Hsipaw State
label: shan states
description: Hsipaw State, historically known as Ong Pawng, was a prominent Shan principality situated along the Nam Tu river valley in the Northern Shan States. Subjugated by the expanding Toungoo monarch King Bayinnaung in 1558, Hsipaw was integrated into the Burmese tributary network as a dependent vassal realm. Administered by hereditary saophas residing at Hsipaw town, the principality contributed military contingents to imperial Burmese campaigns while maintaining internal customary governance until British subjugation in 1886. \n\n Status: Vassal Shan state of Burma; Capital: Hsipaw; Common languages: Shan, Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Saopha; Established: 1558; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Laihka State
label: shan states
description: Laihka State was an autonomous Shan hill principality located in the central plateau of the Southern Shan States along the Nam Teng river basin. Conquered in 1558 during the eastward expansion of King Bayinnaung of Burma, Laihka became an obedient vassal state within the Toungoo and subsequent Konbaung empires. Governed by a line of hereditary saophas from the palace at Laihka, the realm retained local administrative institutions and religious customs until British paramountcy was imposed in 1886. \n\n Status: Vassal Shan state of Burma; Capital: Laihka; Common languages: Shan, Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Saopha; Established: 1558; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Mongmit State
label: shan states
description: Mongmit State, recorded in Burmese as Momeik, was an important Shan principality located in the Northern Shan States north of the ruby-rich Mogok plateau. Subjugated in 1558 following King Bayinnaung's triumphant royal campaigns across the Shan hills, Mongmit rendered regular tribute and auxiliary troops to the Burmese crown. The hereditary saophas preserved domestic jurisdiction over the fertile valley of the Nam Mit until the third Anglo-Burmese War brought the territory under British imperial control in 1886. \n\n Status: Vassal Shan state of Burma; Capital: Mongmit; Common languages: Shan, Burmese, Palaung; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Saopha; Established: 1558; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Principality of Mingrelia
description: The Principality of Mingrelia, known historically as Odishi or Samegrelo, was an autonomous Georgian realm established in western Transcaucasia following the fragmentation of the Kingdom of Georgia. Ruled by the noble Dadiani dynasty from their ancestral residence at Zugdidi, the principality commanded fertile agricultural lowlands along the Black Sea coast. The mtavaris of Mingrelia preserved sovereign autonomy against Ottoman expansion and rival Georgian houses until Prince Grigol Dadiani concluded a treaty of Russian protectorate in 1804. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Zugdidi; Ruling dynasty: Dadiani; Common languages: Mingrelian, Georgian; Religion: Georgian Orthodoxy; Government: Principality; Ruler title: Mtavari; Established: 1558; Disestablished: 1804; Succeeded by: Russian Empire

name: Province of Macau
label: concessions in china
description: The Province of Macau was an enduring Portuguese settlement and colonial possession situated on the western side of the Pearl River Delta in southern China. Leased from the Ming dynasty in 1557 following annual land rent payments, the port city functioned under mixed Portuguese municipal administration and Chinese sovereignty for three centuries. The territory developed into a pivotal global trading nexus linking Europe, Japan and the Americas before transitioning to full Portuguese colonial governance in the nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Portuguese settlement; Capital: Macau; Official languages: Portuguese, Chinese; Religion: Roman Catholicism, Buddhism; Government: Colonial administration; Legislature: Leal Senado; Historical era: Age of Discovery; Established: 1558; Currency: Macanese pataca

name: Wa States
label: shan states
description: The Wa States comprised a rugged cluster of autonomous highland chieftaincies inhabited by the Wa people in the mountainous frontier region between the Salween River and the Mekong. Brought into nominal tributary dependence following King Bayinnaung's Shan campaigns in 1558, the isolated hill communities rendered token fealty to Burmese royal authority. The mountainous topography allowed Wa chieftains to maintain customary self-rule, ritual traditions and fierce defensive independence until the area was integrated into British Burma in 1886. \n\n Status: Vassal confederation of Burma; Capital: None (decentralised); Administrative seat: Pangkham; Common languages: Wa, Shan; Religion: Traditional animism; Government: Chieftainships; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1558; Disestablished: 1886

name: Wuntho State
label: shan states
description: Wuntho State was a fortified Shan principality positioned in Upper Burma between the Ayeyarwady and Chindwin rivers. Subdued in 1558 by the expanding Toungoo armies of King Bayinnaung, the state was incorporated as a strategic frontier vassal charged with guarding royal interior communications. Administered by local hereditary sawbwas from the town of Wuntho, the state retained broad domestic jurisdiction and supplied military levies to the Burmese crown until British troops annexed the territory in the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Vassal Shan state of Burma; Capital: Wuntho; Common languages: Burmese, Shan; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Sawbwa; Established: 1558; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Yawnghwe State
label: shan states
description: Yawnghwe State was one of the largest and most influential Shan principalities in the Southern Shan States, centred around the waters of Inle Lake. Subdued by King Bayinnaung during the military pacification of the Shan plateau in 1558, the state became a prized vassal of the Burmese monarchy. Its saophas governed from their grand palace at Nyaungshwe, maintaining internal law and overseeing lake trade while fulfilling tributary obligations until entering British protectorate agreements in 1886. \n\n Status: Vassal Shan state of Burma; Capital: Nyaungshwe; Common languages: Shan, Intha, Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Saopha; Established: 1558; Disestablished: 1886; Succeeded by: British Burma

name: Lan Na Kingdom
description: The Lan Na Kingdom was a Tai monarchical realm in northern Thailand that fell under Burmese suzerainty when King Bayinnaung conquered the fortified capital of Chiang Mai on 2 April 1558. Subordinated as a tributary mandala under the Toungoo and later Konbaung dynasties, the kingdom retained native princes who oversaw local administration and Buddhist religious foundations. Burmese hegemony ended on 15 January 1775, when local Lan Na chieftains allied with King Taksin of Thonburi to expel Burmese garrisons. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of Burma; Capital: Chiang Mai; Common languages: Northern Thai, Burmese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Mandala monarchy; Ruler title: King; Established: 2 April 1558; Disestablished: 15 January 1775; Succeeded by: Siam

name: Chiang Hung State
label: shan states
description: Chiang Hung State, also known as Sipsong Panna, was an autonomous Tai Lue principality located in the forested mountains of the upper Mekong River in present-day southern Yunnan. Following King Bayinnaung's northeastern campaigns in 1559, the kingdom accepted Burmese vassal status while concurrently maintaining tributary relations with Ming and Qing China under the tusi system. Governed by hereditary chao pha rulers from the city of Chiang Hung, the state balanced multi-imperial dependencies until deeper administrative integration in 1851. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Chiang Hung; Common languages: Tai Lue, Burmese, Chinese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Chao Pha; Established: 1559; Disestablished: 1851; Historical region: Xishuangbanna

name: Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek
label: holy roman empire
description: The Bishopric of Osel-Wiek was an independent prince-bishopric and imperial estate within the Holy Roman Empire, encompassing the western Estonian islands of Saaremaa and Hiiumaa alongside adjacent coastal mainland territories. Headquartered at Haapsalu and Kuressaare castles, the theocratic principality briefly exercised unfettered sovereign authority amidst the geopolitical chaos of the early Livonian War. Faced with devastating Russian advances and internal Protestant reformation, Prince-Bishop Johannes V von Munchhausen negotiated the sale of the diocese to King Frederick II of Denmark. \n\n Status: Prince-bishopric of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Haapsalu; Common languages: Low German, Estonian, Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical elective principality; Ruler title: Prince-Bishop; Disestablished: 1560; Succeeded by: Danish Estonia

name: Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek
label: holy roman empire
description: The Bishopric of Osel-Wiek functioned as a Baltic protectorate and appanage of the Danish Crown following its purchase in 1560 by King Frederick II for his younger brother, Duke Magnus of Holstein. Governed from the island stronghold of Kuressaare on Saaremaa, the territory gave Denmark an essential commercial and naval base in the eastern Baltic. Danish ducal administration persisted until the conclusion of the Torstenson War, when the Treaty of Bromsebro in August 1645 ceded the islands to the Swedish Empire. \n\n Status: Protectorate of Denmark; Capital: Kuressaare; Common languages: Low German, Danish, Estonian; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Princely appanage; Ruler title: Duke; Established: 1560; Disestablished: 13 August 1645; Succeeded by: Swedish Empire

name: Gorkha Kingdom
description: The Gorkha Kingdom was an independent hill monarchy in the central Himalayas founded in 1559 by Prince Dravya Shah, a younger royal son from Lamjung. Governed from the fortified palace citadel of Gorkha Durbar, the kingdom gradually expanded by integrating neighbouring valleys and organising disciplined infantry regiments. Under the leadership of King Prithvi Narayan Shah after 1743, the state launched extensive conquest campaigns that captured the Kathmandu Valley, culminating in the formal emergence of the unified Kingdom of Nepal. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Gorkha; Ruling dynasty: Shah; Common languages: Khas, Nepali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Established: 1560; Disestablished: 1770; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal

name: County of Tassarolo
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Tassarolo was an autonomous imperial fief within the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Ligurian Apennine hills between Genoa, Piedmont and Montferrat. Granted imperial immediacy by Emperor Ferdinand I on 30 May 1560, the territory was ruled by the noble Spinola di Luccoli family from their medieval castle. Despite its diminutive geographic footprint, the county gained widespread commercial prominence across northern Italy through its active sovereign mint until passing under Savoyard suzerainty in 1736. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Tassarolo; Ruling dynasty: Spinola; Common languages: Italian, Ligurian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Count; Established: 30 May 1560; Disestablished: 1736; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Sardinia

name: Mukunda Dynasty
description: The Mukunda Dynasty, founded by King Mukunda Deva of the Chalukya lineage, was a sovereign Hindu regime that ruled the historic realm of Odisha from the fortress city of Cuttack. Seizing the throne in 1560 following the turbulent demise of the Bhoi dynasty, Mukunda Deva allied with the Mughal Emperor Akbar to resist the northern expansion of the Bengal Sultanate. The dynasty's independent rule ended abruptly in 1568 when Sultan Sulaiman Karrani invaded Odisha, resulting in the king's death in battle. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Cuttack; Ruling dynasty: Chalukya; Common languages: Odia, Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Gajapati; Established: 1561; Disestablished: 1569; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Bengal

name: Sheka
description: Sheka, also remembered as the Kingdom of Shakacho, was an independent monarchy situated in the lush montane rainforests of south-western Ethiopia. Ruled by hereditary sovereigns known as the tato from their royal residence at Anderaccha, the state preserved distinct cultural institutions and maintained vibrant trade in highland coffee, honey and ivory. Sheka vigorously defended its mountain perimeter against regional Oromo movements for centuries until imperial Ethiopian forces under Emperor Menelik II conquered and incorporated the realm in 1899. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Anderaccha; Common languages: Shakacho, Omotic languages; Religion: Traditional beliefs, Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Tato; Historical era: Pre-colonial; Disestablished: 1899; Succeeded by: Ethiopian Empire

name: Duchy of Estonia
description: The Duchy of Estonia was an overseas dominion of the Swedish Empire comprising northern Estonia, established on 4 June 1561 when the nobility of Harjumaa, Virumaa and the town of Reval submitted to King Eric XIV. Administered by a Swedish governor-general residing at Toompea Castle in Reval, the province retained its Baltic German legal traditions, Lutheran faith and noble land privileges. Swedish rule endured for one hundred and sixty years until the territory was surrendered to Russia under the Treaty of Nystad. \n\n Status: Dominion of the Swedish Empire; Capital: Reval; Official languages: Swedish, German; Common languages: Estonian, German, Swedish; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Governorate-general; Representative title: Governor-General; Established: 4 June 1561; Disestablished: 10 September 1721; Succeeded by: Russian Empire

name: Duchy of Courland and Semigallia
description: The Duchy of Courland and Semigallia was an autonomous Baltic vassal state created under the Pactum Subiectionis of 28 November 1561, when Gotthard Kettler, the last Master of the Livonian Order, secularised his lands under Polish-Lithuanian suzerainty. Governed from its palace capital at Mitau, the Lutheran duchy maintained its own Landtag, legal apparatus and maritime fleet, establishing overseas trading colonies in Tobago and the Gambia River. The state retained Polish vassal status until incorporated into the Russian Empire during the Third Partition of Poland. \n\n Status: Vassal state of Poland-Lithuania; Capital: Mitau; Ruling dynasty: Kettler, Biron; Common languages: German, Latvian; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Feudal duchy; Ruler title: Duke; Established: 28 November 1561; Disestablished: 28 March 1795; Succeeded by: Russian Empire

name: Duchy of Livonia
description: The Duchy of Livonia was an autonomous Baltic province established on 28 November 1561 by the Treaty of Vilnius following the collapse of the Livonian Confederation. Held in condominium by the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Kingdom of Poland, the duchy encompassed southern Estonia and northern Latvia, preserving Baltic German municipal privileges and Lutheran worship. Prolonged Polish-Swedish warfare culminated in the Truce of Altmark on 26 September 1629, which partitioned the territory and transferred northern Livonia to Swedish imperial rule. \n\n Status: Vassal dependency of Poland-Lithuania; Capital: Fellin; Official languages: Latin, Polish, German; Common languages: German, Latvian, Estonian; Religion: Lutheranism, Roman Catholicism; Government: Principality; Established: 28 November 1561; Disestablished: 26 September 1629; Succeeded by: Swedish Livonia

name: Free Imperial City of Riga
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Riga was an autonomous mercantile city-state on the Baltic coast that refused to submit to the Treaty of Vilnius upon the dissolution of the Livonian Confederation in 1561. Asserting sovereign immediacy under the Holy Roman Empire, the city was governed by a German-dominated municipal town council and maintained flourishing Hanseatic maritime trade along the Daugava River. Riga preserved its independence for nearly two decades until submitting to King Stephen Bathory of Poland-Lithuania under the Treaty of Drohiczyn in January 1581. \n\n Status: Free imperial city; Capital and largest city: Riga; Common languages: Low German, German, Latvian; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Oligarchic city republic; Legislature: Riga Town Council; Established: 28 November 1561; Disestablished: 14 January 1581; Succeeded by: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth

name: Denmark-Norway (Military Occupation)
description: Denmark-Norway Military Occupation comprised the foreign territories and contested frontier zones held under martial governance by the armed forces of the Dano-Norwegian dual monarchy during major regional wars. First instituted during the Northern Seven Years' War following the capture of Alvsborg fortress in September 1563, martial commands supervised occupied fortifications along the Kattegat and Baltic coastlines. These temporary occupation regimes enforced military requisitions and secured strategic maritime checkpoints until diplomatic peace treaties restored territorial boundaries. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: None (decentralised); Common languages: Danish, Norwegian, German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 4 September 1563; Disestablished: 13 December 1570; Succeeded by: Sweden

name: Marquisate of Castiglione del Lago
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Castiglione del Lago was an autonomous noble fief situated on the western shore of Lake Trasimeno in central Italy, elevated to a marquisate on 19 November 1563 by Pope Pius IV. Held by the illustrious della Corgna family, the dynasty resided in the grand Renaissance Palazzo Ducale and exercised judicial and civil authority over the lake settlements. The independent status of the marquisate terminated on 12 December 1647 following the extinction of the male lineage, whereupon the territory was absorbed into the Papal States. \n\n Status: Marquisate; Capital: Castiglione del Lago; Ruling dynasty: Della Corgna; Common languages: Italian, Umbrian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Marquis; Established: 19 November 1563; Disestablished: 12 December 1647; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Burma (Military Occupation)
description: Burma Military Occupation designated the extensive zones in Mainland Southeast Asia held under direct martial administration by imperial Burmese forces during expansive military expeditions. Beginning with King Bayinnaung's triumphant initial capture of Siamese border settlements in 1564, Burmese garrison commanders requisitioned supplies, managed military logistics and enforced martial law over subjugated valleys. These temporary wartime administrations secured strategic crossing corridors along the Tenasserim frontier and Chao Phraya basin during recurrent conflicts against Ayutthaya and neighbouring states. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: None (decentralised); Common languages: Burmese, Siamese Thai, Mon; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Military command; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1564; Head of state: King of Burma; Historical region: Indochina

name: Mong Mao State
label: shan states
description: Mong Mao State was a historic Tai principality established in the Ruili River basin along the upland frontier connecting Upper Burma with Yunnan. Subjugated by the Toungoo military expeditions of King Bayinnaung in 1564, the state was integrated as a tributary border vassal under the Burmese crown. Governed by native saophas from their fortified valley settlements, Mong Mao navigated competing political demands from both the Burmese court and Ming imperial officials until sustained military conflicts dismantled its autonomy around 1605. \n\n Status: Vassal Shan state of Burma; Capital: Selan; Common languages: Old Shan, Burmese, Chinese; Religion: Theravada Buddhism, Tai folk religion; Government: Hereditary principality; Ruler title: Saopha; Established: 1564; Disestablished: 1605; Succeeded by: Toungoo Burma, Ming China

name: Ayutthaya Kingdom
description: The Ayutthaya Kingdom was an illustrious Siamese monarchy in the Chao Phraya river basin that was reduced to tributary vassalage by King Bayinnaung of Burma on 1 March 1564. Governed from the moated island capital of Ayutthaya by royal nominees and tributary kings, the court rendered annual tribute and dispatched royal princes as hostages to the Toungoo capital of Pegu. Siamese vassal status endured through repeated conflicts until Prince Naresuan formally declared the restoration of Siamese independence at Krang on 3 May 1584. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of Burma; Capital: Ayutthaya; Common languages: Siamese Thai; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Mandala monarchy; Ruler title: King; Established: 1 March 1564; Disestablished: 3 May 1584; Succeeded by: Ayutthaya Kingdom (Independent)

name: French Florida
description: French Florida was an early colonial enterprise founded on 22 June 1564 by French Huguenot settlers led by Rene Goulaine de Laudonniere on the banks of the St Johns River. Centred on the triangular earthen stronghold of Fort Caroline, the colony aimed to provide a secure Protestant refuge and challenge Spanish dominance across the Caribbean Sea lanes. The vulnerable settlement succumbed on 20 September 1565 when Spanish troops under Pedro Menendez de Aviles launched a surprise overland assault, destroying the garrison. \n\n Status: French colony; Capital: Fort Caroline; Common languages: French, Timucua; Religion: Calvinism, Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Historical era: Age of Discovery; Established: 22 June 1564; Disestablished: 20 September 1565; Succeeded by: Spanish Florida

name: Sultanate of Bijapur, Sultanate of Ahmadnagar, Sultanate of Golconda and Sultanate of Bidar (Military Occupation)
description: The Deccan Sultanates Military Occupation comprised the temporary martial control exercised jointly over the Vijayanagara heartland following the decisive Battle of Talikota on 23 January 1565. Formed by an allied confederacy of the sultans of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar, the invading coalition marched upon the imperial capital of Vijayanagara on 1 February 1565. For several weeks, allied troops ransacked the fortified city and systematically dismantled its palaces before withdrawing their armies back to their respective Deccan realms. \n\n Status: Joint military occupation; Administrative seat: None (decentralised); Common languages: Persian, Kannada, Telugu, Dakhini; Religion: Islam; Government: Allied military command; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1 February 1565; Disestablished: 1 March 1565; Historical region: Deccan

name: County of Königsegg-Rothenfels
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Konigsegg-Rothenfels was an immediate imperial state of the Holy Roman Empire located in the scenic Allgau alpine foothills of south-western Bavaria. Governed by the Swabian noble House of Konigsegg from their administrative seat at Immenstadt, the territory exercised sovereign jurisdiction and held representation within the Swabian Imperial Circle. The counts preserved autonomous rule through centuries of regional warfare until Count Franz Fidelis sold the county to Austria in 1804, after which France ceded it to Bavaria in 1805. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Immenstadt; Ruling dynasty: House of Konigsegg; Common languages: Swabian German, German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Count; Established: 1566; Disestablished: 1805; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bavaria

name: Kingdom of Alo
description: The Kingdom of Alo, historically known as Tu`a or the Kingdom of Futuna, was a sovereign Polynesian realm established on the eastern half of Futuna and neighbouring Alofi Island. Governed by a traditional paramount ruler titled the Tu`i Agaifo, the monarchy maintained political authority through a council of village chiefs and customary land tenure. The kingdom preserved its sovereign isolation and maritime traditions until 29 November 1887, when its leadership signed a protectorate treaty with France alongside adjacent Sigave. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Alo; Common languages: Futunan, French; Religion: Traditional beliefs, Roman Catholicism; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Tu`i Agaifo; Historical era: Pre-colonial; Established: 1566; Disestablished: 29 November 1887; Succeeded by: French Wallis and Futuna

name: Kingdom of Mysore
description: The Kingdom of Mysore was a formidable southern Indian monarchy founded by the Hindu Wadiyar dynasty in the southern Deccan plateau, which attained full sovereign independence after the collapse of the Vijayanagara Empire in 1565. Governed from Srirangapatna, the realm expanded dramatically across Karnataka during the seventeenth century through extensive administrative and fiscal centralisation. Under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan in the late eighteenth century, Mysore became a militarised power renowned for rocketry, battling the British East India Company until Tipu's fall in May 1799. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Srirangapatna; Ruling dynasty: Wadiyar; Common languages: Kannada, Persian, Hindustani; Religion: Hinduism, Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja, Sultan; Established: 1566; Disestablished: 4 May 1799; Succeeded by: Princely State of Mysore

name: Tsangpa
label: tibetan era of fragmentation
description: The Tsangpa Dynasty was a powerful Tibetan royal dynasty established in west-central Tibet, originating from the fortress palace of Samdruptse at Shigatse. Founded by Karma Tseten, a former governor under the Rinpungpa, the regime patronised the Karma Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism while vigorously contesting political supremacy against the Gelug school backed by Mongol factions. Tsangpa hegemony reached its zenith under Phuntsok Namgyal and Karma Tenkyong before collapsing in 1642 following an invasion by Gushi Khan of the Khoshut Khanate. \n\n Status: Royal dynasty; Capital: Samdruptse; Common languages: Tibetan; Religion: Tibetan Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Desi; Historical era: Tibetan era of fragmentation; Established: 1566; Disestablished: 1643; Succeeded by: Khoshut Khanate

name: Kingdom of Garo
label: kingdoms in the gibe region
description: The Kingdom of Garo, historically known as Bosha, was an independent Sidama monarchy situated on the northern periphery of the Gojeb River in the Gibe region of south-western Ethiopia. Ruled by the Bosha dynasty from their fortified mountain settlements, the kingdom maintained traditional monarchical structures and preserved Christian practices amidst expanding regional Oromo migrations. Garo maintained its sovereign identity through armed resistance until it was overwhelmed and incorporated into the neighbouring Kingdom of Jimma in 1884. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Bonga; Ruling dynasty: Bosha; Common languages: Bosha, Omotic; Religion: Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity, Traditional beliefs; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Tato; Historical era: Pre-colonial; Disestablished: 1884; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Jimma

name: Landgraviate of Hesse-Darmstadt
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine
description: The Landgraviate of Hesse-Darmstadt was an immediate principality of the Holy Roman Empire created in 1567 upon the partition of Hesse following the death of Landgrave Philip I. Governed by Landgrave George I and his descendants from the residence city of Darmstadt, the state embraced Lutheranism and expanded its territory through the Upper Hesse inheritance. The landgraviate endured the devastation of the Thirty Years' War and French Revolutionary conflicts until Napoleon dissolved the Holy Roman Empire in August 1806, elevating Hesse-Darmstadt into a Grand Duchy. \n\n Status: Landgraviate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Darmstadt; Ruling dynasty: House of Hesse; Common languages: German, Hessian dialects; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Landgrave; Established: 1568; Disestablished: 13 August 1806; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Hesse

name: Landgraviate of Hesse-Kassel
label: holy roman empire
description: The Landgraviate of Hesse-Kassel was a major Protestant principality of the Holy Roman Empire established in 1567 when Landgrave William IV inherited the northern portion of Hesse upon his father's death. Governed from the fortified city of Kassel, the landgraviate developed a disciplined standing army, adopting Calvinism in 1605 and famously subsidising its treasury through foreign mercenary military contracts. The state maintained significant diplomatic influence throughout central Europe until the imperial recess of February 1803 elevated the ruler to Imperial Elector, creating the Electorate of Hesse. \n\n Status: Landgraviate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Kassel; Ruling dynasty: House of Hesse; Common languages: German, Hessian; Religion: Calvinism, Lutheranism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Landgrave; Established: 1568; Disestablished: 25 February 1803; Succeeded by: Electorate of Hesse

name: Landgraviate of Hesse-Marburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Landgraviate of Hesse-Marburg was an autonomous imperial principality created in 1567 under the testamentary partition of Hesse for Landgrave Louis IV, the second son of Philip the Magnanimous. Encompassing Upper Hesse around the castle city of Marburg and the towns of Giessen and Nidda, the state maintained Lutheran orthodoxy and supported the venerable University of Marburg. Louis died without surviving issue in 1604, triggering a prolonged dynastic inheritance dispute that ultimately partitioned Hesse-Marburg between Hesse-Kassel and Hesse-Darmstadt. \n\n Status: Landgraviate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Marburg; Ruling dynasty: House of Hesse; Common languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Landgrave; Established: 1568; Disestablished: 1605; Succeeded by: Hesse-Kassel, Hesse-Darmstadt

name: Landgraviate of Hesse-Rheinfels
label: holy roman empire
description: The Landgraviate of Hesse-Rheinfels was a short-lived principality of the Holy Roman Empire established in 1567 for Philip the Younger, the third son of Landgrave Philip I of Hesse. Centred on the imposing stronghold of Rheinfels Castle overlooking Sankt Goar on the Rhine, the state derived significant revenues from lucrative riverine toll rights. Philip governed the territory until his death without male heirs in November 1583, after which the principality was partitioned and absorbed by his elder brother William IV of Hesse-Kassel. \n\n Status: Landgraviate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Sankt Goar; Ruling dynasty: House of Hesse; Common languages: German; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Landgrave; Established: 1568; Disestablished: 1584; Succeeded by: Landgraviate of Hesse-Kassel

name: Duchy of Salci
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Salci was an autonomous imperial and papal enclave situated along the Chiana valley borderland between Umbria and Tuscany, centred on the fortified castle hamlet of Salci near Fabro. Raised to the status of a duchy in 1568 by Pope Pius V in favour of Lucrezia Bandini, the territory was subsequently inherited and administered by the patrician Bonelli family. The duchy exercised local civil jurisdiction and customs autonomy until formal mediatisation and reincorporation into the Papal States in October 1816. \n\n Status: Fief of the Holy Roman Empire and Papacy; Capital: Salci; Ruling dynasty: Bandini, Bonelli; Common languages: Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal duchy; Ruler title: Duke; Established: 1569; Disestablished: 23 October 1816; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Kingdom of Portugal (Military Occupation)
description: The Kingdom of Portugal Military Occupation designated overseas expeditionary garrisons and contested territories placed under direct martial governance by Portuguese royal armed forces during foreign campaigns. Beginning with maritime incursions along the Zambezi valley and the Indian Ocean coastline in 1569, Portuguese captains-general exercised martial law over occupied settlements and trading posts. These temporary military command structures secured transit waterways, requisitioned supplies and defended strategic crown fortresses until normal civil administration or diplomatic treaties re-established stable territorial boundaries. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: None (decentralised); Common languages: Portuguese; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military administration; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1569; Ruler title: King of Portugal; Historical region: Portuguese Overseas Empire

name: Langkat Sultanate
description: The Langkat Sultanate was a sovereign Malay Muslim kingdom situated along the northeastern coastal plains of Sumatra, established in 1568 by Raja Dewa Shahdan. Governed from the riverine capital of Tanjung Pura, the sultanate commanded rich agricultural lowlands and prospered through trade in pepper, timber and riverine goods across the Strait of Malacca. Langkat preserved its sovereign independence against Acehnese and Siak dominance for centuries until signing a formal treaty of vassalage with the Dutch East Indies government in 1888. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Tanjung Pura; Ruling dynasty: Dewa; Common languages: Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Established: 1569; Disestablished: 1888; Succeeded by: Dutch East Indies

name: Sultanate of Pajang
description: The Sultanate of Pajang was a short-lived Javanese Islamic state in central Java, established in 1568 by Sultan Hadiwijaya, widely known as Jaka Tingkir, following the civil wars of the collapsing Demak Sultanate. Governed from its inland palace near modern Surakarta, Pajang shifted the political centre of gravity from coastal ports to the fertile agricultural heartland of the Solo river basin. Dynastic succession turmoil following Hadiwijaya's death enabled his adopted vassal, Sutawijaya, to usurp authority and establish the Mataram Sultanate in 1587. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Pajang; Common languages: Javanese; Religion: Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan; Preceded by: Demak Sultanate; Established: 1569; Disestablished: 1587; Succeeded by: Mataram Sultanate

name: Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania
description: The Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, known as the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, was a federative bi-confederate dual monarchy inaugurated on 1 July 1569 by the Union of Lublin. Spanning vast territories from the Baltic Sea to the Ukrainian steppes, the state operated under a unique noble democracy where an elected monarch shared legislative power with the General Sejm. Characterised by remarkable religious tolerance and noble civil liberties, the Commonwealth flourished as one of Europe's largest powers before facing internal paralysis and external partitions. \n\n Status: Commonwealth dual monarchy; Capital: Warsaw; Official languages: Polish, Latin; Common languages: Ruthenian, Lithuanian, German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Elective monarchy and noble democracy; Legislature: General Sejm; Established: 1 July 1569; Currency: Zloty, Thaler

name: Grand Duchy of Tuscany
label: holy roman empire
description: The Grand Duchy of Tuscany was an influential sovereign Italian monarchy established on 27 August 1569 when Pope Pius V issued a papal bull elevating Cosimo I de' Medici following the conquest of Siena. Governed from Florence, the grand duchy flourished through Mediterranean naval commerce from Livorno, administrative centralisation and generous artistic patronage. The House of Medici ruled until its extinction in 1737, whereupon the crown passed to the House of Habsburg-Lorraine, which implemented enlightened administrative, agricultural and judicial reforms throughout the territory. \n\n Status: Grand duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Florence; Ruling dynasty: Medici, Habsburg-Lorraine; Official languages: Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Grand Duke; Established: 27 August 1569; Currency: Tuscan lira, Tuscan fiorino

name: BaKwêna
description: The BaKwena was an independent sovereign chiefdom of the Sotho-Tswana people established in the Kalahari transitional savannahs of modern south-western Botswana. Governed by hereditary kgosi from their capital at Molepolole, the society was structured around extensive cattle pastoralism, communal assembly traditions and veneration of the crocodile totem. Under the visionary nineteenth-century leadership of Kgosi Sechele I, the BaKwena successfully repelled Boer expansionism and built diplomatic ties with British authorities, culminating in incorporation into the Bechuanaland Protectorate in 1885. \n\n Status: Kingdom; Capital: Molepolole; Common languages: Setswana; Religion: Traditional beliefs, Christianity; Government: Traditional monarchy; Ruler title: Kgosi; Historical era: Pre-colonial; Established: 1571; Disestablished: 23 March 1885; Succeeded by: Bechuanaland Protectorate

name: Principality of Transylvania
description: The Principality of Transylvania was an autonomous East Central European state situated across the Carpathian basin, recognised as an Austrian vassal following the 1570 Treaty of Speyer between John Sigismund Zapolya and Maximilian II. Governed from the ducal seat of Alba Iulia, the realm maintained a diet composed of the Three Nations and granted legal recognition to four religious confessions. Habsburg suzerainty was reaffirmed under the 1699 Treaty of Karlowitz, lasting until the suppression of Rakoczi's War of Independence in 1711. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of Austria; Capital: Alba Iulia; Common languages: Hungarian, German, Latin, Romanian; Religion: Calvinism, Lutheranism, Roman Catholicism, Unitarianism; Government: Elective principality; Legislature: Diet of Transylvania; Established: 1571; Disestablished: 29 April 1711; Succeeded by: Habsburg Monarchy

name: Principality of Transylvania
description: The Principality of Transylvania operated as a self-governing tributary vassal state of the Ottoman Empire following the election of Stephen Bathory by the estates at Alba Iulia in March 1571. Paying an annual tribute to the Sublime Porte in exchange for non-interference in domestic governance and religious freedom, the principality served as a crucial buffer between Ottoman and Habsburg realms. Transylvania experienced a golden age of cultural and institutional development under native princes, successfully preserving Protestant autonomy across the eastern Carpathian basin. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of the Ottoman Empire; Capital: Alba Iulia; Common languages: Hungarian, German, Latin, Romanian; Religion: Calvinism, Lutheranism, Roman Catholicism, Unitarianism; Government: Elective principality; Ruler title: Prince; Established: 14 March 1571; Disestablished: 11 November 1606; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Crimean Khanate (Military Occupation)
description: The Crimean Khanate Military Occupation comprised the vast swath of central Russian lands temporarily subjected to martial devastation and cavalry control following the daring campaign of Khan Devlet I Giray in May 1571. Mobilising a massive host of Crimean Tatar and Nogai horsemen, the khan outmanoeuvred Muscovite frontier garrisons, capturing and burning the suburbs of Moscow on 24 May 1571. Tatar forces held operational dominance over the southern steppe approaches until their decisive defeat at the Battle of Molodi in August 1572. \n\n Status: Military occupation; Administrative seat: None (decentralised); Common languages: Crimean Tatar, Russian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military cavalry command; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 15 May 1571; Disestablished: 1 September 1572; Head of state: Devlet I Giray

name: Nagasaki
description: Nagasaki was a prominent maritime trading post and Jesuit mission base situated on a sheltered deep-water harbour in south-western Kyushu. Formally established in 1571 under agreements with the Christian daimyo Omura Sumitada, the port served as the exclusive terminus for the Portuguese black ship trade carrying Chinese silk and Japanese silver. Although Toyotomi Hideyoshi placed the town under direct ducal administration in 1587, Portuguese merchants retained commercial rights until the Tokugawa shogunate enforced maritime seclusion in the late 1630s. \n\n Status: Portuguese trading post; Administrative seat: Nagasaki; Common languages: Portuguese, Japanese; Religion: Roman Catholicism, Buddhism; Government: Commercial factory; Historical era: Sengoku to Edo period; Established: 1572; Disestablished: 1640; Succeeded by: Tokugawa Shogunate

name: Dutch Rebels
description: The Dutch Rebels, organised under the leadership of William the Silent, Prince of Orange, constituted the autonomous revolutionary insurgent polity of the Low Countries during the opening decade of the Eighty Years' War. Sparked on 1 April 1572 by the surprise capture of the port of Brielle by the Sea Beggars, rebellious towns across Holland and Zeeland repudiated Spanish military tyranny while defending historic municipal charters. The rebel regime coordinated naval warfare, financial levies and civil administration until formally consolidating through the 1579 Union of Utrecht. \n\n Status: Insurgent confederation; Capital: Brielle; Common languages: Dutch; Religion: Calvinism, Roman Catholicism; Government: Revolutionary council; Head of state: William the Silent; Historical era: Dutch Revolt; Established: 1 April 1572; Disestablished: 23 January 1579; Succeeded by: Union of Utrecht

name: Duchy of Saxe-Coburg-Eisenach
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Saxe-Coburg-Eisenach was an autonomous Ernestine Wettin state of the Holy Roman Empire established in 1572 under the Treaty of Erfurt following the partition of Saxe-Weimar. Co-ruled by Duke John Casimir and Duke John Ernest from their palaces in Coburg and Eisenach, the territory spanned scattered territories in Upper Franconia and Thuringia. The brothers amicably divided their patrimony in 1596, though the duchy was briefly re-established in the 1630s before its final partition between Saxe-Altenburg and Saxe-Weimar. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Coburg; Ruling dynasty: House of Wettin (Ernestine); Common languages: German, Upper Saxon; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Established: 1573; Disestablished: 1639; Preceded by: Saxe-Weimar

name: Duchy of Saxe-Weimar
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine
description: The Duchy of Saxe-Weimar was an immediate imperial state of the Holy Roman Empire located in Thuringia, governed by the genealogically senior Ernestine branch of the House of Wettin from the residence town of Weimar. Created following the 1572 Division of Erfurt, the duchy stood as a steadfast champion of the Lutheran Reformation, fostering humanist culture, music and the nearby University of Jena. The realm absorbed neighbouring territories over subsequent centuries until merging dynastically with Saxe-Eisenach in 1741 to form Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Weimar; Ruling dynasty: House of Wettin; Common languages: German, Thuringian; Religion: Lutheranism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Established: 1573; Disestablished: 1742; Succeeded by: Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach

name: Chhaya State
description: Chhaya State was an independent Rajput principality established on the Kathiawar peninsula in western Gujarat, ruled by the Jethwa clan. Following the sack of their ancient maritime capital at Ghumli, the Jethwa rulers transferred their royal seat to Chhaya, erecting fortified palaces and securing revenues from coastal commerce and fertile agricultural holdings. The state maintained sovereign autonomy through complex diplomatic manoeuvring against neighbouring Jamnagar and Junagadh until 1785, when the rulers relocated their principal seat to nearby Porbandar. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Chhaya; Ruling dynasty: Jethwa Rajput; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Rana; Established: 1575; Disestablished: 1786; Succeeded by: Porbandar State

name: Galkot
label: nepal petty kingdoms
description: Galkot was an autonomous hill principality governed by Khas royalty in the Gandaki river watershed of modern Baglung District in western Nepal. As an active constituent of the Chaubisi Rajya confederation of twenty-four states, the kingdom guarded strategic mountain routes linking Pokhara with the western highlands. Galkot preserved its domestic independence through strong hilltop fortifications until 1787, when the expanding armed forces of the Gorkha monarchy conquered the principality and incorporated its territory into the Kingdom of Nepal. \n\n Status: Principality; Capital: Galkot; Common languages: Khas, Nepali; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1575; Disestablished: 1787; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Nepal; Historical region: Gandaki

name: Powhatan Confederacy
description: The Powhatan Confederacy was a sovereign alliance of over thirty Algonquian-speaking Indigenous nations occupying the coastal plain of Tsenacommacah in modern Tidewater Virginia. Led by paramount chief Wahunsenacawh from his royal village of Werowocomoco, the confederacy maintained sophisticated agricultural production, hunting reserves and riverine canoe transport. Confrontations with expanding English settlers from Jamestown escalated into multiple Anglo-Powhatan wars, culminating in catastrophic population decline from warfare and European diseases until the Treaty of Middle Plantation formally subordinated the tribes in 1677. \n\n Status: Indigenous confederacy; Capital: Werowocomoco; Common languages: Powhatan; Religion: Traditional animism; Government: Paramount chieftainship; Ruler title: Mamanatowick; Historical era: Early modern period; Established: 1575; Disestablished: 28 May 1677; Succeeded by: Colony of Virginia

name: Colony of Angola
description: The Colony of Angola, officially known as Portuguese West Africa, was an Atlantic colonial possession founded in 1575 by Paulo Dias de Novais around the port settlement of Sao Paulo da Assuncao de Luanda. Established initially to secure captive labour for Portuguese sugar plantations in Brazil, colonial authorities operated fortified coastal enclaves and launched military expeditions against the kingdoms of Kongo, Ndongo and Matamba. Portuguese control gradually expanded into the interior highlands over centuries, persisting until administrative reorganisation established an overseas province in 1951. \n\n Status: Colony of the Portuguese Empire; Capital: Luanda; Official languages: Portuguese; Common languages: Kimbundu, Umbundu, Kikongo; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Colonial governorship; Representative title: Governor-General; Established: 1576; Reorganised: 20 October 1951; Currency: Portuguese real, Angolan escudo

name: Kingdom of Imereti
description: The Kingdom of Imereti was a Christian Georgian monarchy in western Transcaucasia that was forced into tributary vassalage to the Ottoman Empire following Ottoman victories during the Caucasian campaigns of the late 1570s. Governed from the ancient royal citadel of Kutaisi by the Bagrationi dynasty, the kingdom was subjected to heavy annual tributes of coin, horses and enslaved captives. Despite recurrent Ottoman punitive expeditions and civil strife among regional nobles, Imeretian kings defended their ecclesiastical autonomy until seeking Russian imperial protection in 1804. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Ottoman Empire; Capital: Kutaisi; Ruling dynasty: Bagrationi; Official languages: Georgian; Religion: Georgian Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Established: 1 September 1576; Disestablished: 25 April 1804; Succeeded by: Russian Empire

name: County of Hohenzollern-Haigerloch
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Hohenzollern-Haigerloch was an immediate principality of the Holy Roman Empire located in south-western Germany, created in 1576 upon the partition of the County of Zollern. Governed by Count Christoph of Hohenzollern and his successors from the hilltop castle at Haigerloch, the Catholic enclave exercised territorial sovereignty along the Eyach River basin. The senior Haigerloch line became extinct upon the death of Count Christoph in 1623, after which the county was annexed and incorporated into neighbouring Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen in 1624. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Haigerloch; Ruling dynasty: House of Hohenzollern (Swabian); Common languages: Swabian German, German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Count; Established: 1577; Disestablished: 1624; Succeeded by: Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen

name: County of Hohenzollern-Hechingen
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Hohenzollern-Hechingen was a sovereign imperial fief situated in Swabia in south-western Germany, formed in 1576 through the tripartite division of the ancestral County of Zollern. Governed by Count Eitel Frederick IV from the fortress of Hohenzollern and the town of Hechingen, the dynasty maintained staunch loyalty to the Catholic Habsburg emperors throughout the Reformation. The territory retained its comital status and imperial immediacy until 1623, when Count Johann Georg was elevated to imperial princely rank, establishing the Principality of Hohenzollern-Hechingen. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Hechingen; Ruling dynasty: House of Hohenzollern; Common languages: Swabian German, German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Count; Established: 1577; Disestablished: 1624; Succeeded by: Principality of Hohenzollern-Hechingen

description: The County of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen was an autonomous imperial estate in the Swabian Jura of south-western Germany, established in 1576 following the division of the older County of Zollern. Ruled by Count Karl II from the imposing Sigmaringen Castle above the Danube River, the comital dynasty administered a compact Catholic territory holding full voting rights in the Swabian Imperial Circle. The comital phase concluded in 1623 when Emperor Ferdinand II raised Count Johann to hereditary princely dignity, transforming the domain into the Principality of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Sigmaringen; Ruling dynasty: House of Hohenzollern; Common languages: Swabian German, German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Count; Established: 1577; Disestablished: 1624; Succeeded by: Principality of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen

name: Principality of Arenberg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Principality of Arenberg was an immediate state of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Eifel mountains of the modern Rhineland-Palatinate. Originally a medieval lordship, the territory was elevated to an imperial princely county in 1576 under Margaret de La Marck-Arenberg and her husband Jean de Ligne. Governed from the fortified ancestral seat of Aremberg Castle, the princes exercised sovereign territorial rights and held a seat in the Imperial Diet until being elevated to a full imperial duchy in 1644. \n\n Status: Principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Aremberg; Ruling dynasty: House of Arenberg; Common languages: German, Moselle Franconian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Prince; Established: 1577; Disestablished: 1646; Succeeded by: Duchy of Arenberg

name: Shamkhalate of Tarki

description: The Shamkhalate of Tarki was a prominent Kumyk feudal monarchy situated on the Caspian littoral of the north-eastern Caucasus, centred on the ancient stronghold of Tarki. Following diplomatic overtures in 1576, the ruling shamkhals accepted nominal vassalage to the Safavid Empire, acting as Iranian march wardens against northern steppe powers and the Russian Empire. The shamkhals preserved extensive domestic sovereignty and dominated regional Dagestani principalities until the 1813 Treaty of Gulistan permanently transferred sovereign authority over the Caspian lowlands to the Russian crown. \n\n Status: Vassal principality of Persia; Capital: Tarki; Ruling dynasty: Shamkhal; Common languages: Kumyk, Persian, Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Shamkhal, Vali of Dagestan; Established: 1577; Disestablished: 24 October 1813; Succeeded by: Russian Empire

name: Duchy of Sabbioneta
label: holy roman empire
description: The Duchy of Sabbioneta was an autonomous imperial principality of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Po River valley of Lombardy, created on 18 November 1577 when Emperor Rudolf II elevated Vespasiano Gonzaga to duke. Envisioned as a Renaissance ideal city, Sabbioneta was meticulously constructed with star-shaped bastions, orthogonal streets, a grand ducal palace and the Teatro all'Antica. The sovereign duchy preserved internal independence amidst surrounding Spanish Milanese and Mantuan territories until the death of Duchess Anna Carafa in 1689. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Sabbioneta; Ruling dynasty: Gonzaga; Common languages: Italian, Lombard; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Duke; Established: 18 November 1577; Disestablished: 1 July 1689; Succeeded by: Spanish Habsburg Monarchy

name: Sultanate of Harar
description: The Sultanate of Harar was a sovereign Islamic city-state on the eastern Ethiopian plateau that emerged following the disintegration of the Adal Sultanate. When Sultan Muhammad Jasa relocated his primary court to the Afar oasis of Aussa in 1577, local Harari amirs established an autonomous regime behind the formidable defensive stone walls of Jugol in Harar. Serving as a premier commercial and scholarly redoubt, the sultanate maintained independent regional trade in coffee and textiles until integrating into broader regional confederacies in the late 1590s. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Harar; Common languages: Harari, Arabic, Somali; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Sultan, Amir; Preceded by: Adal Sultanate; Established: 1578; Disestablished: 1596; Historical region: Horn of Africa

name: Vijaynagar State
description: Vijaynagar State, historically known as Pol State, was an autonomous Rajput principality established in 1577 in the rugged forested hills of the Mahi Kantha region of north-eastern Gujarat. Founded by Rao Chandrasenji of the Rathore dynasty following his displacement from Idar, the state established its fortress capital at Vijaynagar. The rulers defended their highland valleys against neighbouring Mughal and Maratha incursions, preserving local sovereign governance until entering into formal subsidiary treaty agreements with the British East India Company in 1851. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Vijaynagar; Ruling dynasty: Rathore Rajput; Common languages: Gujarati; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Rao; Established: 1578; Disestablished: 1851; Succeeded by: British East India Company

name: Kingdom of Kartli
description: The Kingdom of Kartli was an eastern Georgian Christian monarchy that fell under the suzerainty of the Ottoman Empire on 24 August 1578 following Lala Mustafa Pasha's successful Caucasian campaign. Headquartered at Tbilisi, the Bagrationi court was forced to accept Ottoman garrisons, remit annual tribute and accommodate Turkish military control along the Kura river valley. Despite foreign vassalage, local kings, including Simon I, waged relentless guerrilla warfare and maintained clandestine Safavid ties until the expulsion of Ottoman forces during the campaigns of Shah Abbas I in 1604. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Ottoman Empire; Capital: Tbilisi; Ruling dynasty: Bagrationi; Common languages: Georgian, Persian; Religion: Georgian Orthodoxy; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Established: 24 August 1578; Disestablished: 1604; Succeeded by: Safavid Empire

name: Kingdom of Kakheti
description: The Kingdom of Kakheti was an eastern Georgian monarchy situated along the Alazani River valley that submitted to Ottoman vassalage in September 1578 during the Ottoman-Safavid War. Governed from the fortified palace city of Gremi by King Alexander II of the Bagrationi dynasty, the kingdom preserved internal agricultural stability and thriving silk production by agreeing to pay annual tribute to Istanbul. The vassalage endured until 1604, when Safavid military counter-offensives and internal dynastic turmoil disrupted Ottoman dominance across eastern Transcaucasia. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Ottoman Empire; Capital: Gremi; Ruling dynasty: Bagrationi; Common languages: Georgian, Persian; Religion: Georgian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: King; Established: 1 September 1578; Disestablished: 1604; Succeeded by: Safavid Empire

name: Sultanate of Sulu
description: The Sultanate of Sulu was a powerful sovereign maritime Muslim state encompassing the Sulu Archipelago, coastal western Mindanao and northern Borneo, centred on the port capital of Jolo. Gaining full independence from the Sultanate of Brunei in 1578, the realm was governed by the Sultan of Sulu in conjunction with the Ruma Bechara council of nobles. Sulu dominated maritime trade in pearls, sea cucumber and spices, mounting fierce naval resistance against repeated Spanish colonial invasions until capitulating under the 1851 peace treaty. \n\n Status: Sultanate; Capital: Jolo; Ruling dynasty: Royal House of Sulu; Common languages: Tausug, Sama, Malay; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Unitary Islamic monarchy; Legislature: Ruma Bechara; Established: 1579; Disestablished: 30 April 1851; Succeeded by: Spanish East Indies

name: Union of Utrecht
description: The Union of Utrecht was a sovereign confederation of rebellious northern provinces of the Low Countries, established on 23 January 1579 in the chapter house of Utrecht Cathedral. Formed by Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht, Gelderland and neighbouring regions as a mutual defence pact against Spanish royal oppression, the agreement established joint systems for military defence, taxation and religious policy. Operating under the leadership of William the Silent, this alliance served as the constitutional foundation that directly produced the independent Dutch Republic upon the 1581 Act of Abjuration. \n\n Status: Confederation; Capital: Utrecht; Common languages: Dutch; Religion: Calvinism, Roman Catholicism; Government: Confederal republic; Head of state: William the Silent; Historical era: Dutch Revolt; Established: 23 January 1579; Disestablished: 26 July 1581; Succeeded by: United Provinces of the Netherlands

name: Tinos

description: Tinos was an autonomous insular Aegean maritime domain centred on the impregnable mountaintop fortress of Exomvourgo in the Cyclades archipelago. Emerging out of the fragmented Frankokratia period and held under direct Venetian administration, the island functioned as an isolated Christian redoubt that sustained local self-governing communes and a flourishing Catholic-Orthodox population. Tinos served as Venice's most vital forward naval lookout and refuge in the Levant, successfully withstanding numerous Ottoman sieges until finally surrendering to an overwhelming Turkish armada in 1715. \n\n Status: Maritime island lordship; Capital: Exomvourgo; Common languages: Greek, Venetian, Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism, Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Oligarchic administration; Historical era: Frankokratia; Established: 1580; Disestablished: 1716; Succeeded by: Ottoman Empire

name: Kingdom of Portugal
description: The Kingdom of Portugal entered a period of dynastic personal union with the Crown of Castile and the Crown of Aragon on 24 October 1580, following the War of the Portuguese Succession and King Philip II's coronation. Governing through the Council of Portugal from Lisbon, the realm preserved its distinct legal codes, monetary systems and global empire across South America, Africa and Asia. Friction over onerous Spanish taxation and naval vulnerabilities culminated on 1 December 1640 in a successful nationalist revolt, restoring an independent Portuguese monarchy under the House of Braganza. \n\n Status: Kingdom in personal union with Spain; Capital: Lisbon; Ruling dynasty: House of Habsburg; Official languages: Portuguese, Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King of Portugal; Established: 24 October 1580; Disestablished: 1 December 1640; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Portugal (Braganza)

name: Emirate of Tagant
description: The Emirate of Tagant was a sovereign nomadic state established in the central Saharan uplands of modern Mauritania, founded by the Idawish confederation of Hassaniya Arab and Berber lineage. Governed by a hereditary emir from key oasis settlements such as Tidjikdja and Tichit, the emirate dominated trans-Saharan caravan routes, date palm agriculture and gum arabic trade. The emirate preserved political autonomy through dynamic alliances and desert warfare against rival emirs until French colonial troops assassinated Emir Bakar Ould Soueid Ahmed and annexed Tagant in 1906. \n\n Status: Emirate; Capital: Tidjikdja; Ruling dynasty: Idawish; Common languages: Hassaniya Arabic, Berber; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Traditional emirate; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: Pre-colonial; Established: 1581; Disestablished: 1906; Succeeded by: French West Africa

name: Macapá
description: Macapa was an English commercial and maritime outpost established along the northern channel of the Amazon River delta in present-day Amapa, northern Brazil. Founded by English merchant-adventurers seeking trading footholds along the Guiana coast and Amazonian waterways, the settlement facilitated barter with indigenous communities for dyewood, tobacco and exotic tropical products. Facing hostile Portuguese counter-expeditions, disease and shifting Tudor-Stuart colonial policies, the English presence was progressively undermined and finally abandoned around March 1603 as Portuguese forces asserted undisputed control over the Amazon mouth. \n\n Status: English colonial trading post; Administrative seat: Macapa; Common languages: English, Tupi; Religion: Protestantism; Government: Commercial factory; Historical era: Elizabethan era; Established: 1581; Disestablished: 24 March 1603; Succeeded by: Portuguese Brazil
